title: Cross-sectional Body Imaging Fellowship
prerequisites: Completed diagnostic radiology residency or equivalent specialist-level knowledge; this self-study course is pitched at resident/fellow level.
Comfort with abdominal and pelvic cross-sectional anatomy, CT/MRI protocols, contrast fundamentals, clinical history review and structured reporting.
Access only to public educational readings/media; case interpretation remains educational and must not involve real patient care.
objectives: Select and justify abdominal/pelvic CT, MRI and ultrasound approaches from clinical question, appropriateness guidance, protocol quality and safety context.
Describe common hepatobiliary, pancreatic, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, pelvic and vascular findings with calibrated differentials and limitations.
Use organ-specific reporting systems such as LI-RADS, PI-RADS and O-RADS MRI only within their intended scope; distinguish Bosniak renal cyst classification.
Interpret time-sensitive findings and communicate limitations/urgent concerns through appropriate supervised/local pathways.
Produce concise structured reports, protocol critiques, conference summaries and quality reflections without claiming procedure competence.
Identify board, accreditation, licensing and training distinctions relevant to abdominal imaging.

units.title: Clinical question, protocol selection, contrast safety
objectives: Frame indication, urgency, prior imaging, modality choice and risk-benefit.
Apply current contrast-risk screening and escalation concepts using institutional policy; distinguish education from authorization.
units.casePractice: For two fictional indications, justify modality and protocol, state the unresolved clinical question, and identify contrast-safety checks without giving patient-specific orders.

assessment.passStandard: Formative rubric only; no credentialing or validated board readiness.

units.title: Cross-sectional anatomy, acquisition and quality
objectives: Use multiplanar anatomy and a repeatable search pattern across abdomen and pelvis.
Recognize phase, motion, coverage and artifact limitations before interpreting.
units.casePractice: Submit a structured search checklist and annotate (in words only) how an acquisition limitation changes confidence.

assessment.passStandard: Formative rubric only; no credentialing or validated board readiness.

units.title: Liver lesion characterization and HCC risk systems
objectives: Describe lesion enhancement and ancillary features on multiphasic CT/MRI.
Use LI-RADS only in the population and modality to which it applies; distinguish diagnosis from indeterminate categories and treatment response.
units.casePractice: Using a linked external teaching case, write a category-focused differential and identify the applicable eligibility context; do not copy the image.

assessment.passStandard: Formative rubric only; no credentialing or validated board readiness.

units.title: Biliary tree, gallbladder and pancreas
objectives: Select US, CT or MRI/MRCP based on clinical variant and timing.
Describe pancreatitis complications, pancreatic cystic/solid lesions and periampullary obstruction while avoiding unsupported certainty.
units.casePractice: Compare two fictional presentations and defend the next modality using the ACR variant rather than a generic rule.

assessment.passStandard: Formative rubric only; no credentialing or validated board readiness.

units.title: Bowel, mesentery and GI oncology
objectives: Interpret bowel obstruction, inflammation, ischemia and trauma using distribution and complications.
Use enterography and staging concepts appropriately; state limits of imaging.
units.casePractice: Build a concise differential from an external case; state one time-critical alternative and one limitation.

assessment.passStandard: Formative rubric only; no credentialing or validated board readiness.

units.title: Renal, adrenal and retroperitoneum
objectives: Choose renal mass characterization sequences and distinguish cystic from solid renal lesions.
Describe adrenal/retroperitoneal findings and incidental findings with management-relevant qualifiers.
units.casePractice: Submit a structured finding-to-differential matrix; apply Bosniak only to cystic renal masses and cite limitations.

assessment.passStandard: Formative rubric only; no credentialing or validated board readiness.

units.title: Prostate MRI and pelvic staging
objectives: Describe multiparametric prostate MRI and PI-RADS terminology.
Avoid transferring prostate criteria to other organs; report local extent and relevant nodes with qualifiers.
units.casePractice: Review an external prostate case and separate lesion category, staging observations and non-imaging uncertainty.

assessment.passStandard: Formative rubric only; no credentialing or validated board readiness.

units.title: Gynecologic and pelvic MRI
objectives: Characterize adnexal lesions using morphology and enhancement.
Use O-RADS MRI as a structured risk stratification framework and state when assessment is incomplete.
units.casePractice: Create a structured report plan for an external teaching case without inferring histology from imaging alone.

assessment.passStandard: Formative rubric only; no credentialing or validated board readiness.

units.title: Abdominal vascular imaging
objectives: Select CTA/MRA protocol and phases for vascular questions.
Describe patency, stenosis, aneurysm, collateralization, and urgent findings with appropriate limits.
units.casePractice: Use a linked case to propose a vascular checklist and state how protocol timing affects interpretation.

assessment.passStandard: Formative rubric only; no credentialing or validated board readiness.

units.title: Emergency imaging, trauma and acute abdomen
objectives: Prioritize life-threatening and time-sensitive findings.
Integrate CT/US/MRI with clinical question, phase and limitations; communicate urgent findings through local escalation policy.
units.casePractice: For fictional vignettes, rank findings by urgency, provide differential and state the communication step (not patient management).

assessment.passStandard: Formative rubric only; no credentialing or validated board readiness.

units.title: Oncology, response assessment and multidisciplinary communication
objectives: Describe staging-relevant anatomy and measurable disease consistently.
Compare like-for-like studies and avoid overstating response; present a concise question-focused conference summary.
units.casePractice: Prepare a one-page fictional tumor-board imaging synopsis with evidence, limitations and questions for the clinical team.

assessment.passStandard: Formative rubric only; no credentialing or validated board readiness.

units.title: Ultrasound, image-guided biopsy interface, reporting and quality
objectives: Explain ultrasound and CT/MR strengths in body imaging.
Describe safe workflow boundaries, target/route planning concepts and reporting/QA without procedural authorization.
units.casePractice: Complete a report audit and protocol critique; identify which steps require supervised, credentialed clinical practice.

assessment.passStandard: Formative rubric only; no credentialing or validated board readiness.

assignment.name: Three-part formative capstone: protocol selection, structured report and multidisciplinary handoff
assignment.instructions: Select one linked authentic de-identified external teaching case (or use an explicitly fictional vignette). Link to it; do not copy images, DICOM or records. Submit a) question-focused protocol rationale and image-quality caveats; b) concise structured observations/differential/report; c) 150-word conference communication including uncertainty, one alternative and a safety/rights reflection. This is not patient care, a clinical report for an actual patient, or authorization to perform procedures.

rubric.criterion: Accurate observations, differential and appropriate system scope
Limitations, safety, uncertainty and evidence use

assignment.feedback: Formative self-assessment; no credentialing or diagnostic competency determination.

assessment.formativeChecks: Twelve original single-best-answer questions with rationales; unit cases, short protocol and report tasks; self-grade against per-unit rubrics.
assessment.summativePlan: Capstone described in assignment, with rubric. Study plan and assessments do not validate readiness for ABR examinations.
assessment.passingClaim: No exam-passing prediction, cut score or guarantee.

studyHours.type: transparent study plan, not verified contact time
studyHours.breakdown: 36.76 observed video hours, approximately 75 hours for readings/notes, 50 hours for case-based reasoning using external linked cases, and 18 hours for assignments/question review. Adjust to learner background. Study time is not a clinical-training equivalence.

mapping.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / The Johns Hopkins Hospital Department of Radiology
mapping.name: Cross-Sectional Body Imaging Fellowship (CT/MRI/US)
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page: advanced body CT, US and MR; 13 blocks of four weeks are stated, but the listed segments (4 MR + 4 CT + 1 cardiothoracic + 2 US + 1 biopsy + 4 elective) sum to 16 blocks. This published inconsistency is unresolved. Page describes daily case/didactic conferences and monthly fellow presentations; full didactic recordings/case volumes are not public.

mapping.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / The Johns Hopkins Hospital Department of Radiology
mapping.name: Body MRI Fellowship (separate clinical variant; not merged)
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page describes a separate 12-month clinical Body MRI fellowship including chest, cardiac, vascular, abdomen, pelvis, prostate and musculoskeletal MRI; separate eligibility and clinical scope. Excluded from this course’s distinct-track hour ledger.

unitMap.text: Clinical question, protocol selection, contrast safety
Cross-sectional anatomy, acquisition and quality
Liver lesion characterization and HCC risk systems
Biliary tree, gallbladder and pancreas
Bowel, mesentery and GI oncology
Renal, adrenal and retroperitoneum
Prostate MRI and pelvic staging
Gynecologic and pelvic MRI
Abdominal vascular imaging
Emergency imaging, trauma and acute abdomen
Oncology, response assessment and multidisciplinary communication
Ultrasound, image-guided biopsy interface, reporting and quality

topicGaps: No full, verified standalone video sequence was found in the counted ledger for structured renal/adrenal protocols and Bosniak framework; case conferences may contain relevant cases but titles do not establish coverage.
No title-level verified recording sequence for prostate MRI/PI-RADS or O-RADS MRI was found; readings and original clip plans cover them.

Need explicit coverage of contrast safety/renal risk, image quality/artifacts, dose optimization, communication/QA, and procedure credentialing boundaries; these are syllabus needs, not verified 36h gap.
No coverage completeness map for ABR core blueprint is publicly available from the selected public recordings; case-session content varies and does not replace supervised fellowship.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.programmeSourceScope: This is an actual clinical physician fellowship track within diagnostic radiology, not a standalone primary physician specialty, degree, or combined-program designation. The official page presents it as a distinct institutional fellowship; no combined programme is identified. The separately listed Hopkins Body MRI clinical fellowship is a distinct institutional track and not merged. Research fellowships, postdoctoral research roles and technologist training are not clinical physician fellowship variants. No combined programme is identified on the official track page. ACGME Abdominal Radiology subspecialty requirements provide a comparator, not evidence that the named Hopkins fellowship is accredited.
sourceCaveats: Johns Hopkins’ page documents a clinical physician Cross-Sectional Body Imaging fellowship spanning CT, MRI, ultrasound, cardiothoracic exposure, image-guided biopsy service and electives. It states “13 blocks of four weeks” while listing 4+4+1+2+1+4=16 blocks; this public-page inconsistency is preserved, not resolved.

Johns Hopkins separately lists a 12-month Body MRI clinical fellowship. It is a distinct institutional track, not merged into this syllabus. Research fellowship roles and technologist training are not physician clinical fellowship variants.

ACGME lists Abdominal Radiology as a radiology subspecialty and posts requirements effective 2026-07-01. Johns Hopkins’ Cross-sectional programme page does not state its individual accreditation status. The directory’s general “ACGME Accredited or Equivalent” label (as noted in packet) is not sufficient to certify this specific programme; individual status remains unverified.

The ABR offers primary Diagnostic Radiology certification and a limited named subspecialty certificate list. Its current list does not include a separate abdominal/body imaging board certificate or exam. ACGME abdominal radiology accreditation is not a separate ABR board exam.

Institutional eligibility statements are not course admission rules and can change. The Hopkins page states candidates must be ABR board-eligible/certified in DR and hold/be eligible for a Maryland permanent medical license.

No patient-specific protocol or care recommendation is provided. Clinical practice should use current institutional policy, current ACR/other authoritative guidance and appropriately credentialed supervision.

Free public media time is based on public YouTube metadata captured 2026-10-07. The 47 generic abdominal case-conference sessions provide abdominal case-based reasoning, but titles alone do not establish coverage of every diagnosis or board domain. ARRS titles support the four explicitly described topic lectures.
Clinical images/case data are linked only to external hosts. No images, DICOM, PHI or patient records are copied into course materials. Free-to-view is not permission to rehost.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult has right-upper-quadrant pain and suspected biliary disease. Ultrasound is negative/equivocal and there is no fever or leukocytosis. Which next imaging option is rated usually appropriate in the ACR variant?

options.text: MRI abdomen with MRCP (with or without IV contrast, per protocol)
Routine dual-phase CT without regard to context
No further imaging is ever appropriate
Prostate MRI

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ACR variant lists MRI abdomen with MRCP, with or without IV contrast, and CT with IV contrast as usually appropriate alternatives. Select with clinical context; this is not a universal rule.

practiceQuestions.stem: For a first presentation of suspected acute pancreatitis within 48–72 hours with classic symptoms and elevated enzymes, which statement matches ACR guidance?

options.text: Multiphasic CT is mandatory in all patients
Abdominal US is usually appropriate; CT/MRI may be appropriate depending on the clinical question
MRI is contraindicated
CT without and with contrast is usually appropriate

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACR rates US usually appropriate in this variant; CT with IV contrast and MRI/MRCP may be appropriate, while CT without-and-with contrast is usually not appropriate.

title: Diagnostic and Nuclear Medical Physics Residency
level: Supplementary non-physician medical-physics residency-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Graduate-level physics, calculus, differential equations, linear algebra and probability/statistics; graduate medical-physics background strongly advised.
Basic anatomy/physiology and radiological/nuclear physics; familiarity with dose units and instrumentation.
This is advanced independent education, not a training-place eligibility guide. No learner is authorized to test clinical equipment or make clinical decisions.
objectives: Explain diagnostic and nuclear imaging physics at a level supporting board-blueprint study and supervised clinical discussion.
Interpret image-quality, detector, dose, correction and QC evidence with explicit assumptions and uncertainty.
Map modality-specific competencies to ABR/ABSNM domains without claiming eligibility or predicting examination success.
Recognize modality safety, professional, privacy and scope boundaries and escalate to qualified local personnel.
Design literature-grounded educational QC and protocol-review exercises; do not apply independently to clinical systems.

units.title: Clinical medical physics practice, radiation quantities, and professional responsibilities
objectives: Distinguish activity, exposure, absorbed dose, equivalent/effective dose and their units; identify when each is clinically meaningful.
Describe how physicists collaborate with radiologists, technologists, nursing, radiation safety and engineering teams without substituting for medical decision-makers.
Apply professional ethics, privacy, uncertainty communication and escalation principles to a hypothetical equipment or dose concern.
topics: Atomic/nuclear foundations; decay and interactions; dosimetry vocabulary; uncertainty; ethics; governance and scope.
boardDomains: ABR Part 1 general/clinical foundations; ABR diagnostic or nuclear Part 2 professional practice; ABSNM general knowledge
units.casePractice: Fictional tabletop: an unexplained exposure-index change is reported; distinguish a measurement issue from patient-care decisions and specify safe escalation.
units.assessment: Short calculation and a 250-word safety/ethics memo; rubric: quantities/units 40%, uncertainty 25%, scope/escalation 25%, citation 10%.

units.title: X-ray production, interaction, detector performance and image quality
objectives: Trace how kVp, filtration, generator waveform, geometry and detector response affect spectrum, contrast, noise and dose.
Use MTF, NPS and DQE conceptually to interpret system trade-offs, while recognizing task dependence.
Explain exposure/deviation index as detector exposure indicators rather than direct patient dose.
topics: Tube output; attenuation; scatter; digital detectors; image quality metrics; exposure index; artifacts.
boardDomains: ABR diagnostic Part 2: general radiography, detectors and image quality; ABR Part 1 general
units.casePractice: Review linked institutional educational cases or a phantom scenario; propose a controlled test of exposure-index drift without altering live clinical protocols.
units.assessment: One-page image-quality/dose trade-off analysis; rubric: physics 40%, metric interpretation 30%, safe recommendations 20%, reproducibility 10%.

units.title: Digital radiography, mammography, fluoroscopy and interventional imaging
objectives: Compare acquisition chains and performance tests for general radiography, mammography and fluoroscopy.
Interpret dose-area product/kerma-area product, reference air kerma and fluoroscopy time with limitations.

topics: CR/DR; AEC; mammography and stereotactic systems; fluoroscopy; interventional dose; displays; QC.
boardDomains: ABR diagnostic Part 2: radiography, mammography, fluoroscopy, patient/staff dose

units.title: Computed tomography: acquisition, reconstruction, dose and protocol optimization

boardDomains: ABR diagnostic Part 2: CT, dosimetry, image quality and QC

units.title: Nuclear instrumentation, counting statistics and gamma-camera quality assurance
objectives: Describe scintillation detectors, collimators, energy windows, dead time and count statistics.

unitMap.text: Clinical medical physics practice, radiation quantities, and professional responsibilities
coveredTopics: Atomic/nuclear foundations; decay and interactions; dosimetry vocabulary; uncertainty; ethics; governance and scope.

unitMap.text: X-ray production, interaction, detector performance and image quality
coveredTopics: Tube output; attenuation; scatter; digital detectors; image quality metrics; exposure index; artifacts.

unitMap.text: Digital radiography, mammography, fluoroscopy and interventional imaging
coveredTopics: CR/DR; AEC; mammography and stereotactic systems; fluoroscopy; interventional dose; displays; QC.

unitMap.text: Computed tomography: acquisition, reconstruction, dose and protocol optimization
coveredTopics: CT system geometry; helical acquisition; reconstruction; artifacts; CTDIvol/DLP; size-specific dose; pediatric optimization; QC.

unitMap.text: Nuclear instrumentation, counting statistics and gamma-camera quality assurance
coveredTopics: Gamma camera; well counter/dose calibrator; survey meters; dead time; energy spectra; QC; records.

unitMap.text: Radiopharmaceutical production, decay, detection and imaging workflow
coveredTopics: Radionuclides and decay; production; generators; radiopharmaceuticals; dose calibrator; gamma-camera basics; safety.

unitMap.text: SPECT, PET and hybrid reconstruction, corrections and quantitative imaging
coveredTopics: SPECT projection/reconstruction; PET coincidence; TOF; resolution recovery; attenuation/scatter/random corrections; SPECT/CT, PET/CT and PET/MR; SUV caveats.

unitMap.text: Image quality, pediatric imaging and dose optimization
coveredTopics: Noise/resolution trade-offs; observer/task; pediatric optimization; protocol review; dose/risk communication.

unitMap.text: MRI physics, safety, ultrasound and multimodality informatics
coveredTopics: MRI signal and sequences; gradient/RF hazards; implants; ultrasound; DICOM/PACS/RIS/HL7; image processing; workstation QC.

unitMap.text: Radiation protection, shielding, surveys and regulatory quality systems
coveredTopics: Radiation protection; occupational/public exposure; shielding; fetal dose concerns; contamination and sealed sources; QA audits; compliance.

unitMap.text: Internal dosimetry and radiopharmaceutical therapy physics
coveredTopics: MIRD schema; quantitative SPECT/PET; calibration; segmentation; time integration; dose-volume; uncertainty; radiopharmaceutical therapy.

unitMap.text: Clinical operations, validation, research, teaching and board-domain integration
coveredTopics: Acceptance testing; clinical research; data mining; reproducibility; privacy; professional communication; board blueprint review; lifelong learning.

topicGaps: Verified video ledger now includes the original nine IAEA nuclear-medicine lectures and 11 additional IAEA AI-for-medical-physicists recordings (AI radiation-therapy episode excluded). The AI series adds profession, data, statistics, ethics, clinical implementation, radiomics, diagnostic-AI and validation coverage, but does not substitute for modality-specific instruction.

Diagnostic radiology modality-specific public lecture hours remain insufficiently represented in the verified ledger: x-ray production/detectors, mammography, fluoroscopy, CT acquisition/reconstruction/dosimetry, ultrasound, MRI physics/safety, shielding, and commissioning/QC. The IAEA diagnostic handbook, AAPM resources and ACR guidance offer readings, not observed video hours.

Nuclear medicine instrument, SPECT/PET and pediatric optimization coverage retains the original nine IAEA recordings, but internal dosimetry, therapy physics, regulatory practice, shielding and hands-on acceptance/commissioning are not comprehensively represented by verified recordings.

Verified free external runtime is 14:29:16.624 (14.487951 hours); the actual gap to 36 hours is 21:30:43.376 (21.512049 hours). Newly authored scripts and future production plans do not count as rendered hours.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

American Board of Radiology (ABR) — Nuclear Medical Physics
American Board of Science in Nuclear Medicine (ABSNM) — Nuclear Medicine Physics & Instrumentation

boardStatus.physicianSpecialty: No: this is not a physician residency or physician specialty and has no physician specialty board examination.
boardStatus.medicalPhysicsCredential: Separate medical-physics/scientific certifications exist. ABR has medical physics Part 1, specialty Part 2 (including Diagnostic Medical Physics and Nuclear Medical Physics), and Part 3 oral examination. ABSNM administers general and specialty examination components for nuclear-medicine science. Its current Nuclear Medicine Physics & Instrumentation page specifies related graduate education and supervised/practical experience (including dedicated NMPI time); details are not satisfied by this self-study. These are distinct credentials, not physician boards.
boardStatus.institutionalStatement: Boston Children’s program page says graduates are expected to complete board certification in the chosen specialized field through a recognized certifying body, naming ABR, ABSNM or CCPM. The page’s currently described program is 24 months and permits diagnostic or nuclear focus. The ABR states dual diagnostic+nuclear eligibility for a combined 2+1 residency after 36 months; do not infer eligibility for both from the BCH 24-month public description.
boardStatus.eligibilityVerification: Current eligibility is controlled by certifying boards and individual education/training history. A self-study course confers none. CCPM is named by the institution but its route and current eligibility were not independently checked for this curriculum.

medical.boardEligibilityNotice: No eligibility is promised. ABR eligibility requires the board’s education, accredited supervised training and exam requirements; ABR page describes a 2+1/36-month condition for both diagnostic and nuclear specialties. ABSNM has a separate two-part scientific certification exam. Verify current rules directly with the board.

officialProgrammes.institution: Boston Children’s Hospital (joint programme with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Massachusetts General Hospital, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, and Harvard Medical School)
officialProgrammes.name: Diagnostic and Nuclear Medical Physics Residency
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Exact institution-listed name retained. Official page describes a single CAMPEP-accredited joint residency preparing residents to work in a chosen specialized field of Diagnostic Medical Physics or Nuclear Medical Physics. First 16 months: eight two-month rotations (general radiography/mammography; fluoroscopy/interventional; radiation safety; nuclear medicine; CT; MRI; informatics; ultrasound). Last eight months: two advanced rotations; nuclear option emphasizes NM, hybrid imaging and radionuclide therapy in year two. Page states 24-month structure and board certification expectation in chosen specialty. It does not publish a complete lecture syllabus. The page names multiple affiliate institutions; this entry is not separate additional residency variants.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Only the exact BCH-listed, Harvard Medical School-conjoined joint medical-physics residency is evidenced. It is non-physician. The supplied item packet contains no Johns Hopkins offering; this evidence set does not claim that none exists outside the packet. This standalone supplement should not be duplicated as a physician residency or a second Harvard-affiliate variant. Institution page itself lists the affiliate hospitals as above.
sourceCaveats: The official BCH programme web page was fetched and read; its stated 24-month, chosen-specialty structure was not reconciled against ABR’s separate three-year 2+1 dual-specialty eligibility condition. Do not infer dual certification from program title.

CAMPEP standards require at least two years clinical training and three years for a combined imaging+nuclear residency; exact accredited scope/current listing should be verified with CAMPEP and BCH because the BCH page description states current accreditation but 24 months.

BCH page lists exact institutional affiliation with BIDMC, MGH, BWH and Harvard Medical School. It does not establish separate programme offerings at every affiliate. No Johns Hopkins item evidenced in packet.
No public detailed institutional lecture syllabus or case volume was found; no case counts, clinical eligibility, procedural readiness or outcomes beyond figures on the official page are invented.

The ABSNM current page identifies general and specialty examination components and states NMPI education and practical-experience prerequisites; candidate eligibility remains determined by ABSNM and is not conferred by this course.
IAEA public seminar page links nine recordings and download files; public video metadata was checked on 2026-10-07 for each unique recording.
Human clinical review has not been performed; this is independent education and not accredited training, licensure, authorization, or board certification.

medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A trainee reports a scanner CTDIvol as the absorbed dose to a particular child. Which correction is most important?

options.text: CTDIvol is a standardized scanner output index, not an individual patient organ dose.
CTDIvol directly equals effective dose in mSv.
CTDIvol applies only to MRI.
CTDIvol is the dose-area product.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CTDIvol is a standardized CT output measure based on phantom methodology; patient size, anatomy and protocol matter for patient-specific estimates. It is not organ or effective dose.

practiceQuestions.stem: Why should exposure index not be presented as a direct estimate of patient dose in digital radiography?

options.text: It is an indicator related to detector exposure and depends on system-defined conventions and exam factors.
It measures only MRI RF power.
It directly measures organ dose regardless of anatomy.
It has no relationship to image acquisition.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Exposure/deviation indices are detector exposure indicators and require context; they do not directly measure patient organ dose.

practiceQuestions.stem: A gamma-camera uniformity test is outside the site’s approved limit. What is the safest educationally grounded first response?

options.text: Immediately change a clinical acquisition protocol.
Repeat the measurement using the approved method, preserve the result, compare history and escalate under local policy.
Ignore it if a patient scan looks normal.
Declare all prior examinations invalid.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Check setup and reproducibility, document, compare with baselines, and follow facility procedures under qualified physicist supervision. The result alone does not justify broad clinical conclusions.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about PET SUV is most accurate?

options.text: It is an error-free tissue property independent of acquisition.
It can be affected by calibration, uptake time, reconstruction and patient-related factors.
It can only be measured in SPECT.
It proves a diagnosis by itself.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Quantitative metrics depend on acquisition and processing conditions and require clinical interpretation; they do not establish diagnosis alone.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the central distinction between SPECT reconstruction and a planar image?

options.text: SPECT estimates a tomographic activity distribution from multiple projections.
SPECT uses no detector measurements.
Planar imaging is always quantitatively exact.
SPECT eliminates attenuation and scatter automatically.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Tomographic reconstruction estimates a distribution from projection data, with correction and calibration limitations.

practiceQuestions.stem: A pediatric NM protocol review is requested. Which principle is best?

options.text: Copy the adult protocol unchanged to standardize practice.
Optimize for the specific imaging task with age/size-appropriate professional review and applicable local standards.
Reduce activity to zero without considering diagnostic task.
Assume all pediatric exams use identical settings.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Optimization balances diagnostic task, image quality and radiation protection; pediatric protocols require appropriate expert review, not automatic adult transfer.

practiceQuestions.stem: A PET attenuation-correction map is misregistered. What is a likely technical risk?

options.text: Bias in corrected activity distribution and potential artifacts.
No effect, because correction maps cannot change reconstructed values.
Guaranteed elimination of scatter.
Direct measurement of absorbed dose.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Correction assumptions and spatial alignment affect reconstructed values; errors can bias images.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is an appropriate role of an independent study course in MRI safety?

options.text: Authorize a learner to clear implants and operate the scanner independently.
Build conceptual hazard awareness and direct learners to current site procedures and designated MR safety leadership.
Replace device labeling and local review.
Certify clinical competence.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Independent education cannot replace current device-specific, institutional safety review, supervised competency or role authorization.

practiceQuestions.stem: For internal dosimetry in radiopharmaceutical therapy, why might serial quantitative imaging be relevant?

options.text: It can inform time-activity estimates used in absorbed-dose calculations, subject to calibration, segmentation and model uncertainty.
It guarantees a uniform absorbed dose in all tissues.
It replaces clinical judgement and regulatory oversight.
It makes activity measurement unnecessary.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Patient-specific dosimetry may use quantitative imaging over time; estimates depend on acquisition and modeling assumptions and do not independently direct treatment.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes this program’s relationship to board eligibility?

options.text: Completing this self-study course guarantees ABR certification.
A program’s completion and published board rules are distinct; only the certifying board determines current candidate eligibility.
All clinical physics tracks have one identical physician board exam.
A single specialty exam automatically awards dual certification.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The course is independent self-study and confers no eligibility. ABR rules specify education, supervised accredited training and exam steps; ABSNM has its own certification examination for nuclear medicine science.

assignment.title: Integrated emergency call simulation (educational, fictional)
assignment.instructions: For each of three fictional referral scenarios (multisystem trauma; acute dyspnea; abdominal pain in pregnancy), submit (1) clinical question and missing context, (2) modality/protocol rationale referencing a current source, (3) ordered search checklist, (4) prioritized findings and differential, (5) limitations, (6) concise report, and (7) urgent communication plan. No real patient data/images; do not use to direct patient care.

rubric.appropriateness_and_context: 0–4: identifies variant, missing clinical facts, protocol and evidence limits
rubric.interpretation_and_search: 0–4: systematic search and prioritization; differentiates finding from inference
rubric.communication: 0–4: concise actionable report and documented closed loop
rubric.source_and_safety: 0–4: current appropriate citations, rights compliance, no care directive

assignment.passingStandard: No validated cut score; peer/instructor rubric is formative and not a board predictor.

assessment.formative: 10 original MCQs in this version plus unit retrieval prompts and written readouts; revise source-sensitive answers against current guidelines.
assessment.summativePlan: Three case reports and oral-call simulation scored with assignment rubric, plus a short reflective error-analysis. No assessment is validated for credentialing, licensure, or board prediction.
assessment.questionContent: Original educational questions; not official ABR content.

studyHours.plan: Plan 120 self-study hours: 36h original specialty video production target (currently not ready), 48h linked readings and guideline work, 24h linked case interpretation, 8h question review and 4h reflection/assignment. These are planning hours, not observed completed content.

medical.trackType: Non-ACGME clinical physician fellowship (independent educational curriculum; not a clinical fellowship)
boardNames: American Board of Radiology (ABR) — Diagnostic Radiology primary specialty certification; no separate Emergency Radiology exam/subspecialty certification identified
medical.boardStatus: Emergency radiology is a physician clinical subspecialty practice/fellowship track, but ABR’s official list of subspecialty certifications does not list an Emergency Radiology examination. This course maps learning to broad ABR Diagnostic Radiology knowledge domains only; it is not an ABR-approved blueprint and does not establish board eligibility. No separate emergency radiology board exam identified as of 2026-10-07. ACGME’s official radiology page likewise lists recognized radiology subspecialty categories without Emergency Radiology; this confirms this offering should not be represented as an ACGME subspecialty-accredited programme.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: ABR Diagnostic Radiology certification eligibility is determined solely by ABR and requires the applicable accredited training/exam steps. MGB explicitly describes this one-year fellowship as non-ACGME. Completion of this independent course confers no board eligibility, certificate or credential.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Exact official item variant is MGB/MGH/BWH joint Emergency Radiology Fellowship. MGB page describes one year and non-ACGME status. The page names separate campus histories but does not present separate active applications/programmes in the current integrated programme description. It is a physician subspecialty fellowship, not a research-only postdoc, non-physician course, or generic directory category. No Emory/Johns Hopkins/Harvard separate emergency-radiology programme variants were in the supplied packet; no variant invented.
sourceCaveats: Current MGB page and official board sources were read directly.
Search and source fetch do not establish video playback; YouTube metadata extraction returned bot/sign-in prompts, HTTP 403/429 and no observed runtime, so candidate videos are uncounted.

The AAR curriculum page lists 29 emergency-specific lecture titles, but individual embeds, video durations and playback access could not be verified via stateless tooling; no course-wide six-hour assumption was counted.
Public programme pages do not reveal actual protected teaching/case logs or clinical hours; no case volumes, clinical outcomes, eligibility guarantees or training equivalence are asserted.

ABR current page lists available specialty subspecialty examinations; absence of Emergency Radiology from that list supports no separate ABR exam found, not a claim about every non-ABR credential worldwide.
ACR/EAST clinical recommendations are dated and variant-specific; readers must check the live guideline and local policy before any clinical use.
Human clinical review not performed; no real patient case/images were copied or rehosted.

ACGME radiology overview lists subspecialty categories; emergency radiology is not listed there. Programme status itself is established directly by MGB page, which explicitly labels its fellowship non-ACGME.

sourceReferences.title: ACOG Diagnostic Imaging During Pregnancy and Lactation

medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 34-year-old after blunt trauma has midline cervical tenderness and meets clinician-applied imaging criteria. What is the ACR usually appropriate initial imaging study?

options.text: CT cervical spine without IV contrast
CTA head and neck for every patient
MRI cervical spine with and without contrast
Plain radiographs only

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACR Acute Spinal Trauma (revised 2024): for adults with acute blunt trauma meeting CCR/NEXUS imaging criteria, CT C-spine without contrast is usually appropriate; CTA is reserved for suspected arterial injury.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which modality is usually appropriate in the ACR variant for suspected ligamentous, spinal cord, or nerve-root injury after spine trauma?

options.text: MRI spine area of interest without IV contrast
CT with and without contrast
CTA spine in all cases
No further imaging ever

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACR Acute Spinal Trauma variant 5 rates MRI spine area of interest without IV contrast usually appropriate when ligamentous/cord/root injury is suspected.

practiceQuestions.stem: A cervical fracture extends into a transverse foramen. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: The fracture proves vertebral artery injury
This pattern may prompt BCVI screening consideration under protocol; it does not itself diagnose vessel injury
No vascular concern is possible if the patient is asymptomatic
MRI is always the initial vascular test

practiceQuestions.rationale: EAST 2020 describes high-risk patterns and recommends CTA screening in high-risk cervical spine injuries; bone findings do not establish the vascular diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the EAST 2020 recommendation for adult blunt polytrauma and BCVI detection?

options.text: Use a screening protocol
Screen only after stroke
Routine stent every detected BCVI
No imaging protocol is useful

practiceQuestions.rationale: EAST recommends using a screening protocol; recommendations are guideline-level evidence and local current pathways matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a trauma head CT, which is the safest reasoning approach to a small hyperdensity near the falx?

options.text: Call acute hemorrhage without checking plane, location, or prior images
Assess morphology, location, multiplanar images, artifacts and differential, then state calibrated certainty
Ignore it because falx calcification is always normal
Infer anticoagulation status from density

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACR Head Trauma gives appropriateness guidance; image interpretation must account for mimics and technical context rather than overclaiming.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes CTA from MRI after cervical trauma?

options.text: CTA assesses suspected arterial injury; MRI addresses suspected cord/ligament/root injury in relevant ACR variants
CTA and MRI are interchangeable
MRI is always first for bony fracture
CTA evaluates ligament injury better than MRI

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACR Acute Spinal Trauma separates suspected arterial injury (CTA head/neck usually appropriate) from suspected ligament/cord/root injury (MRI without contrast usually appropriate).

practiceQuestions.stem: A technically limited CTPA shows no central filling defect but poor opacification of segmental branches. Best report approach?

options.text: Declare all pulmonary emboli excluded
Describe contrast/technical limitation and which vascular levels are not reliably assessed
Call a definite segmental PE based on motion
Omit the limitation

practiceQuestions.rationale: Evidence-based reporting principle: qualify the examination and avoid certainty beyond image quality; ACR Appropriateness Criteria are imaging-decision guidance.

practiceQuestions.stem: For an emergency imaging report, which workflow best supports patient safety?

options.text: Urgent actionable finding is communicated directly via local closed-loop process and documented
Place a vague note in report only
Assume the ordering clinician will see it eventually
Contact a family member with findings

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACR practice standards and institutional critical-result policies emphasize timely communication; follow local policy.

practiceQuestions.stem: A pregnant patient needs evaluation of possible time-critical abdominal pathology. What should guide modality choice?

options.text: Automatically avoid all imaging
Clarify clinical question, use current evidence-based pathway and optimize modality/protocol with treating team
Use multiphase CT in every case
Use ultrasound even when nondiagnostic and stop

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACR Appropriateness Criteria support condition-specific selection; pregnancy does not justify blanket withholding of indicated diagnostic imaging. Local pregnancy imaging/safety pathways govern.

practiceQuestions.stem: In suspected pediatric appendicitis, what is the appropriate general learning principle?

options.text: Apply adult CT defaults without adjustment
Use age-specific evidence-based appropriateness guidance and consider ultrasound-first pathways where applicable
Assume a normal appendix is never visible
Transfer all responsibility to the imaging report

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACR has separate child appropriateness variants; pediatric modality selection and radiation optimization differ from adult workflows.

title: Emergency and Trauma Imaging Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (supplementary self-study curriculum; non-ACGME official fellowship)-aligned independent study

prerequisites.level: Postgraduate physician/radiology learner; designed as advanced self-study. Not a route into medical school, residency, fellowship or physician licensure.
required: Diagnostic radiology fundamentals: modality, cross-sectional anatomy, contrast principles and structured reporting.
Trauma-team workflow familiarity or a commitment to study with appropriate supervision.
Ability to critically read guidelines and distinguish recommendation from local protocol.
prerequisites.notIncluded: No hands-on scans, supervised interpretation, procedural instruction, patient-care authority, clinical case-volume credit or credential.

objectives: Use a structured, stability-aware approach to emergency and trauma imaging questions.
Interpret publicly sourced trauma imaging educational material while identifying uncertainty and limitations.
Summarize trauma findings clearly and describe safe critical-result communication in a fictional exercise.
Apply current source and licensing checks to case-based learning.
Distinguish the Emory clinical fellowship from independent self-study and ABR board certification.

units.title: Emergency imaging decisions, trauma workflow, and modality selection
objectives: Summarize how hemodynamic state, suspected injury, and care pathway change imaging choices.
Compare trauma-series radiographs, focused ultrasound, CT, CTA, and MRI by question and limitation.
State why guideline recommendations are not substitutes for bedside team decisions.
topics: ACR appropriateness variants and RCR adult workflow
FAST as adjunct; imaging must not delay resuscitation/intervention
boardDomains: General diagnostic radiology: imaging selection, safety, acute care
ACR 2025 adult major blunt trauma variants
casePractice: Construct a modality-selection matrix for a fictional blunt-trauma vignette; do not write a patient-specific recommendation.

units.title: Trauma CT protocol, contrast, search pattern, and communication
objectives: Use a repeatable search pattern for whole-body CT and describe coverage/phase decisions as protocol- and patient-dependent.
Prioritize actionable findings and communicate uncertainty, critical results, and follow-up needs.
Describe the distinction between preliminary communication and a final report.
topics: Contrast reaction readiness and risk conversation
Primary survey/preliminary report and final report
Structured search, discrepancy review, handoff, audit
boardDomains: General DR: safety, image interpretation, reporting, professionalism
casePractice: Draft a fictional two-stage communication note for a hypothetical trauma CT, explicitly marking unresolved findings.
units.assessment: Rubric: sequence completeness 30%; key actionable findings 30%; uncertainty 20%; communication and safety 20%.

units.title: Head, brain, face, and skull-base trauma
objectives: Identify major acute CT head injury patterns and state what CT does not exclude.

BCVI CTA screening criteria are protocol-dependent

mapping.name: Emergency and Trauma Imaging Fellowship
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Emory describes a one-year non-ACGME fellowship. The public page says 44 clinical weeks: 26 weeks at Grady Memorial Hospital and 18 weeks at Emory University Hospital Midtown; it also lists 4 non-clinical/elective weeks, 3 vacation weeks and 1 conference week. Clinical experience across modalities and additional hospitals is described, but the named core weekly allocations are Grady and Emory University Hospital Midtown. Page objectives include emergency/trauma clinical experience, teaching and academic investigation. Applicants must have completed or be scheduled to complete ACGME- or RCPSC-accredited diagnostic radiology residency before fellowship and meet Georgia licensure requirements. These published descriptions are not reproduced training or offered course hours.

boardStatus.currentFinding: As checked 2026-10-07, ABR lists diagnostic radiology certification and the subspecialty certificates neuroradiology, nuclear radiology, pediatric radiology and pain medicine; its no-longer-issued section lists hospice/palliative medicine and vascular/interventional radiology history. Emergency Radiology is not listed as a current or no-longer-issued separate ABR certificate/exam. No separate Emergency Radiology board exam was identified.
boardStatus.examScope: ABR DR initial certification has separate examination and eligibility requirements. This is not an Emory fellowship examination or a specialty-specific Emergency Radiology board.
boardStatus.qualifier: Recheck ABR/ABMS directly before career or credentialing decisions; this finding is limited to the public ABR pages accessed on the date above.

medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This course/fellowship does not establish eligibility for ABR diagnostic radiology certification or any other board. Emory states that this programme is a one-year non-ACGME fellowship; applicants must have completed or be scheduled to complete ACGME- or RCPSC-accredited diagnostic radiology residency and meet Georgia licensure requirements. ABR DR certification has its own accredited-training, exam and licensure requirements. No Emergency Radiology-specific ABR exam/certificate was found on the public ABR pages checked 2026-10-07.

officialProgrammes.name: Emergency and Trauma Imaging Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Emory describes a one-year non-ACGME fellowship. The public page says 44 clinical weeks: 26 weeks at Grady Memorial Hospital and 18 weeks at Emory University Hospital Midtown; it also lists 4 non-clinical/elective weeks, 3 vacation weeks and 1 conference week. Clinical experience across modalities and additional hospitals is described, but the named core weekly allocations are Grady and Emory University Hospital Midtown. Page objectives include emergency/trauma clinical experience, teaching and academic investigation. Applicants must have completed or be scheduled to complete ACGME- or RCPSC-accredited diagnostic radiology residency before fellowship and meet Georgia licensure requirements. These published descriptions are not reproduced training or offered course hours.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Only the specific Emory clinical physician fellowship attached in the item packet is included. It is a post-residency physician fellowship, not a residency, generic directory label, combined board program, research-only postdoc, non-physician imaging track, or separate board exam. The public page says non-ACGME. No Harvard or Johns Hopkins variant was identified for this named item; this record does not claim one.
sourceCaveats: Emory page describes a one-year non-ACGME fellowship with stated clinical/elective weeks; listed weeks sum to 52, while fellowship title/current Fellows section wording may vary over time. This is a public programme description, not an independently verified current contract or rotation schedule.
ABR exam formats, board eligibility and certificate offerings change. Recheck official ABR pages for actual candidate decisions. This course cannot confer eligibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adult with major blunt trauma is described as hemodynamically stable. Which initial imaging statement best reflects the ACR 2025 Major Blunt Trauma criteria?

options.text: CT whole body with IV contrast is usually appropriate in the stable, otherwise unspecified variant.
MRI of the abdomen and pelvis is usually appropriate as first-line imaging.
Noncontrast whole-body CT is preferred to evaluate vascular injury.
The ACR criteria require one identical protocol for every mechanism and patient.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2025 ACR stable adult major blunt trauma variant rates whole-body CT with IV contrast usually appropriate. This is a guideline category for a defined scenario, not a universal order independent of clinical circumstances or local pathway.

practiceQuestions.stem: For an adult with major blunt trauma who is hemodynamically unstable, which statement is most accurate under the ACR 2025 initial-imaging variant?

options.text: Whole-body CT with IV contrast is categorized as may be appropriate; trauma-series radiography is usually appropriate.
MRI is usually appropriate and must precede resuscitation.
Noncontrast whole-body CT is usually appropriate.
No imaging is ever appropriate.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACR lists trauma-series radiography as usually appropriate and whole-body CT with IV contrast as may be appropriate in the unstable adult variant. Timing and modality are context-dependent and must not delay immediate life-saving care.

practiceQuestions.stem: A hemodynamically stable adult has suspected blunt liver trauma. Which modality statement is supported by the WSES 2020 guideline?

options.text: Contrast-enhanced CT is the diagnostic gold standard in stable trauma patients.
Ultrasound excludes all solid-organ injury.
MRI is mandatory before CT.
Anatomic grade alone determines management.

practiceQuestions.rationale: WSES states contrast CT is the gold standard in hemodynamically stable patients and that admission diagnostic method depends on hemodynamic status. Grading does not replace clinical context.

practiceQuestions.stem: A trauma CT request is made for suspected blunt cerebrovascular injury. Which approach is best supported by the open BCVI review?

options.text: Consider CTA for patients meeting defined clinical or imaging screening risk factors; do not screen indiscriminately using a single isolated low-risk feature.
Use MRI as the universal initial screening test.
A normal neck radiograph excludes BCVI.
All trauma patients must receive CTA regardless of protocol.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The review discusses screening criteria and CTA as a first-line screening modality for patients with specific signs/risk factors; local up-to-date screening pathways govern. A single isolated seat-belt abrasion was not a sufficient criterion in the review.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner sees isolated soft-tissue signal on MRI after cervical trauma without clear structural failure. What is the safest interpretation principle?

options.text: Signal change alone does not necessarily establish mechanical instability; correlate with anatomy, clinical context and other imaging.
Any edema proves a complete ligament rupture.
MRI is never useful after trauma.
Normal radiographs exclude all ligamentous injury.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The Radiology Assistant review explicitly notes controversy and indeterminate significance for some isolated MRI soft-tissue findings. Avoid overcalling; interpret in context.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which communication principle is described in the RCR 2024 major adult trauma guidance?

options.text: Provide a provisional primary-survey report promptly and a formal final report within the guidance time standard.
Wait until the next routine report cycle before communicating life-threatening findings.
A preliminary verbal call replaces all documentation.
The guideline establishes one identical workflow for all jurisdictions.

practiceQuestions.rationale: RCR recommends a provisional primary survey report as soon as possible and a final report within one hour of CT acquisition, with consultant/addendum details specified. These are guideline standards and service context matters.

practiceQuestions.stem: The 2025 ACR stable adult major blunt trauma variant includes pregnancy. Which general principle is most appropriate for this learning exercise?

options.text: Do not apply a blanket prohibition; use current pregnancy-specific appropriateness guidance and the clinical question to balance risk and benefit.
All CT is forbidden during pregnancy regardless of injury.
Ultrasound excludes all maternal injury.
Pregnancy requires no change in communication or protocol review.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ACR document includes a specific pregnant-patient variant with multiple modalities. The educational point is individualized risk/benefit and current protocol consultation, not blanket avoidance.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes this Emergency and Trauma Imaging Fellowship from board certification?

options.text: Emory describes a one-year non-ACGME fellowship; ABR DR certification has separate accredited-training and examination requirements.
Completing the fellowship automatically grants ABR DR board eligibility.
Emergency radiology has a separately listed ABR subspecialty board exam.
A self-study course can replace residency.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Emory calls the fellowship non-ACGME. The ABR DR pathway requires clinical year, accredited DR residency or approved alternate pathway, exams, and valid licensure. The ABR subspecialty list checked does not list Emergency Radiology as a separate certificate.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which rights approach is appropriate when assigning a Radiopaedia case for case practice?

options.text: Link students to the source case; do not copy or rehost media without meeting licence terms and proper attribution.
Any free-to-view image can be downloaded and placed in a course.
Remove the case author credit before reuse.
Public access means the images are public domain.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Radiopaedia states CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 terms, requiring attribution, share-alike and noncommercial conditions; it gives examples of uses not permitted without a licence. This course links only and copies no case media.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adult with suspected major blunt chest trauma has findings requiring urgent escalation. Which reporting practice aligns with trauma radiology workflow?

options.text: Prioritize and directly communicate actionable critical findings through the local trauma-team pathway, document communication, and issue the final report.
Rely solely on an unsigned draft in the queue.
Delay notification until every incidental finding is characterized.
Use a fixed protocol irrespective of patient status.

practiceQuestions.rationale: RCR emphasizes timely provisional reporting, final reporting and local protocols/communication; the course trains educational communication habits, not operational authorization.

mapping.institution: Emory University School of Medicine, Department of Radiology and Imaging Sciences
mapping.name: Imaging Informatics Fellowship
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page: one-year hybrid; 50/50 imaging-informatics and clinical-radiology-subspecialty effort; ongoing technical/research/leadership/management curriculum; year-long academic projects, electives and embedded operational technology projects. Applicant must be accepted to both the informatics fellowship and a chosen clinical fellowship. The fellowship page says graduates of ACGME-accredited US or Canadian radiology residencies who are eligible for Georgia licensure; the Division page additionally states ABR certified/eligible and eligible for an unrestricted Georgia license. Fellows fulfill 100% of standard clinical call requirements in their clinical division. These are clinical training/operational commitments, not lecture hours.
mapping.accreditationBoundary: The official fellowship page reviewed does not state ACGME accreditation. Do not infer accreditation, board eligibility, case volume or a standardized rotation list from the title.

topicGaps: No public Emory lecture inventory, didactic-hour total, named clinical rotation schedule, case-volume minimum, or fellowship-to-board guarantee was found; none is inferred.

The 41 unique candidate YouTube recordings have 130,052 indexed seconds (36.1256 hours) of saved search-metadata runtimes, but a prior ordinary watch-page probe produced a LOGIN_REQUIRED bot-verification interstitial. Their playback/free-access status remains unverified, so all contribute zero verified hours; the actual 36.0-hour target gap remains.

No newly found long-form video was eligible to add: NIH VideoCast page disclosed no observed duration in the retrieved page; SIIM on-demand page requires account/member access or a nonmember fee; RSNA/SIIM NIIC has live/recorded instruction but requires registration and does not publicly enumerate recordings and runtimes.

Content mapping is strengthened by five complete scripted episodes on the lifecycle, DICOM/FHIR acceptance tests, dataset provenance, safe data-access requests, and AI evaluation/governance. These are not recordings and do not close the media-hour gap.

Remaining source-supported teaching gaps include detailed reading-room reliability/outage scenarios, full conformance-statement exercises, QI/FMEA worked examples, implementation-specific procurement/requirements, and hands-on local cybersecurity or AI workflow evaluation. The latter require institutional expertise/access and must not be simulated as clinical authorization.

Public recordings and standards do not substitute for supervised local downtime, interface testing, privacy review, cybersecurity response, clinical interpretation, or AI implementation. International and vendor-sponsored AI webinars are discussion sources, not local legal/regulatory determinations.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician fellowship; independent self-study companion
boardNames: American Board of Radiology (DR examination context; no separate Imaging Informatics subspecialty listed)
American Board of Preventive Medicine (Clinical Informatics—separate 24-month ACGME pathway)
American Board of Imaging Informatics (CIIP professional designation; not represented as ABMS physician board certification)
medical.boardStatus: No separate ABR/ABMS Imaging Informatics certificate or board exam was identified. Imaging informatics appears in the 2026 ABR DR Noninterpretive Skills exam content, not as its own exam. ABPM Clinical Informatics is a distinct physician subspecialty certification with a separate board exam/pathway; its ACGME route requires 24 months or longer of ACGME-accredited Clinical Informatics fellowship plus current primary certification. ABII CIIP has its own professional certification exam/qualification rules, but it is not ABMS physician board certification.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent self-study does not create eligibility for any examination, ABR certification, ABPM Clinical Informatics certification, CIIP, state medical licensure, credentialing, radiation authorization or clinical privileges. Emory’s one-year fellowship page does not claim that it is a 24-month ACGME Clinical Informatics fellowship. ABPM’s ACGME Clinical Informatics pathway requires completion of a 24-month (or longer) ACGME-accredited fellowship and current primary certification; verify current requirements directly with ABPM. The ABR DR pathway requires accredited clinical training/residency, examinations and licensure as stated by ABR.

officialProgrammes.institution: Emory University School of Medicine, Department of Radiology and Imaging Sciences
officialProgrammes.name: Imaging Informatics Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page: one-year hybrid; 50/50 imaging-informatics and clinical-radiology-subspecialty effort; ongoing technical/research/leadership/management curriculum; year-long academic projects, electives and embedded operational technology projects. Applicant must be accepted to both the informatics fellowship and a chosen clinical fellowship. The fellowship page says graduates of ACGME-accredited US or Canadian radiology residencies who are eligible for Georgia licensure; the Division page additionally states ABR certified/eligible and eligible for an unrestricted Georgia license. Fellows fulfill 100% of standard clinical call requirements in their clinical division. These are clinical training/operational commitments, not lecture hours.
officialProgrammes.accreditationBoundary: The official fellowship page reviewed does not state ACGME accreditation. Do not infer accreditation, board eligibility, case volume or a standardized rotation list from the title.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The source packet names one official programme: Emory University School of Medicine. This entry does not merge nuclear radiology, PET/CT, theragnostics, generic clinical informatics, or other institutions’ fellowships into it. The official Emory page does not list standardized named rotations or a complete public lecture set; only its described hybrid structure is reported.
sourceCaveats: Official institutional, board, standards, regulatory, and repository sources were opened and reviewed on 2026-10-07; requirements/pages can change and must be rechecked.

The saved 41-recording YouTube search ledger has unique candidate IDs and integer public-index runtime observations, but the stateless watch-page playback check returned a login-required bot-verification interstitial. Public playability/free access was not established; all entries are retained as candidates and excluded from verified hours. No authentication or bypass was attempted. The learner must recheck ordinary free access before use.

No public Emory lecture set, total didactic-hour disclosure, named clinical rotation list, case volume, ACGME status for this fellowship, or fellowship-to-board guarantee was found. Only the official programme page statements are represented.

The Emory fellowship page says graduates of ACGME-accredited US or Canadian radiology residencies eligible for Georgia licensure; the division page adds ABR-certified/eligible and unrestricted Georgia-license wording. These source-specific wordings are preserved separately rather than silently merged.

The ABPM Clinical Informatics 24-month ACGME fellowship pathway is a separate board pathway; current primary certification is required. ABII CIIP is a separate professional certification with its own exam/qualification rules, not ABMS physician board certification.

The supplied outline’s unsupported case-volume benchmarks, broad institutional assertions, dual-board claims and questionable modality/therapy claims were not imported into this Imaging Informatics curriculum.

No proprietary examination content, protected downloads, patient records, fabricated diagnostic scans, unsupervised clinical instruction, treatment recommendation, or local-system deployment instruction is included.

topicGaps: No public Emory lecture inventory, didactic-hour total, named clinical rotation schedule, case-volume minimum, or fellowship-to-board guarantee was found; none is inferred.

The 41 unique candidate YouTube recordings have 130,052 indexed seconds (36.1256 hours) of saved search-metadata runtimes, but a prior ordinary watch-page probe produced a LOGIN_REQUIRED bot-verification interstitial. Their playback/free-access status remains unverified, so all contribute zero verified hours; the actual 36.0-hour target gap remains.

No newly found long-form video was eligible to add: NIH VideoCast page disclosed no observed duration in the retrieved page; SIIM on-demand page requires account/member access or a nonmember fee; RSNA/SIIM NIIC has live/recorded instruction but requires registration and does not publicly enumerate recordings and runtimes.

Content mapping is strengthened by five complete scripted episodes on the lifecycle, DICOM/FHIR acceptance tests, dataset provenance, safe data-access requests, and AI evaluation/governance. These are not recordings and do not close the media-hour gap.

Remaining source-supported teaching gaps include detailed reading-room reliability/outage scenarios, full conformance-statement exercises, QI/FMEA worked examples, implementation-specific procurement/requirements, and hands-on local cybersecurity or AI workflow evaluation. The latter require institutional expertise/access and must not be simulated as clinical authorization.

Public recordings and standards do not substitute for supervised local downtime, interface testing, privacy review, cybersecurity response, clinical interpretation, or AI implementation. International and vendor-sponsored AI webinars are discussion sources, not local legal/regulatory determinations.
