practiceQuestions.stem: A proposed PACS replacement claims it is “DICOM compatible.” What is the best next step before relying on that claim for a local workflow?

options.text: Assume all DICOM implementations interoperate identically.
Request and evaluate the vendor conformance statement, then run a representative acceptance test.
Convert all studies to screenshots before migration.
Test only image display; metadata and workflow are unrelated.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABR guide explains that vendors using DICOM are expected to provide conformance statements detailing their implementation. Compatibility claims must be tested against the intended local workflow; DICOM does not eliminate implementation-specific testing.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement most accurately distinguishes FHIR from DICOM in an imaging enterprise?

options.text: FHIR replaces pixel-image encoding and storage in all imaging systems.
DICOM has no relationship to FHIR resources.
FHIR is a standard for electronic healthcare-information exchange; DICOM remains an imaging standard and is incorporated into imaging-related FHIR resources.
FHIR can be used only for billing.

practiceQuestions.rationale: HL7 describes FHIR as a standard for exchanging healthcare information electronically. DICOM states that it is incorporated in imaging-related HL7 FHIR resources. The standards are complementary, not interchangeable.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional outage, current studies display but priors do not. Which initial response best protects interpretation workflow?

options.text: Tell readers that priors are never needed.
Document the degradation, activate the approved downtime/escalation pathway, and verify patient/study matching before any workaround.
Disable all audit logs to improve speed.
Copy studies to an unmanaged personal drive.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Reading-room availability and order-to-report workflow are ABR informatics domains. A managed escalation and matching verification protects patient safety; bypassing audit and data controls does not.

practiceQuestions.stem: A model has a high internal AUROC on one institution’s retrospective data. What is the strongest next evidence question?

options.text: Whether its intended use, reference standard, relevant subgroups and external or real-world performance have been evaluated.
Whether the model name sounds clinically persuasive.
Whether the training set had the largest possible file size.
Whether it can be installed without user training.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NIST frames AI risk around trustworthiness across design, development, use and evaluation, and FDA GMLP stresses a total-product-lifecycle approach. A single internal discrimination result is not sufficient evidence for local use.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which action is appropriate when learning from TCIA LIDC-IDRI data?

options.text: Try to combine records with outside sources to identify participants.
Rehost the collection without checking data-use conditions.
Use the collection under its stated license, retain its DOI citation, and do not attempt re-identification.
Treat each radiologist annotation as a forced-consensus ground truth.

practiceQuestions.rationale: TCIA prohibits re-identification attempts and requires dataset-specific attribution/licensing review. The LIDC-IDRI description states that readers rendered final opinions without forced consensus; annotations are a learning resource with limits.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner wants to share an institutional DICOM sample in a class forum after removing the patient name from the header. What is the best response?

options.text: One removed field always makes a study de-identified.
Proceed if the learner promises not to mention the hospital.
Do not share it; use approved public data or institutional review. HIPAA de-identification has defined methods and imaging can retain identifying risk.
Convert it to JPEG, which eliminates all privacy considerations.

practiceQuestions.rationale: HHS describes Expert Determination and Safe Harbor as the two Privacy Rule de-identification methods. This independent course prohibits sharing real patient data; format conversion or removing one field is not a substitute for approved review.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABR NIS 6.4 Data Privacy and Security

practiceQuestions.stem: Which item belongs in a pre-deployment plan for a fictional imaging AI tool?

options.text: A claim that vendor authorization alone proves local safety and effectiveness.
Intended use, local acceptance testing, user training, monitoring measures, escalation and a stop/review pathway.
Only a marketing slide deck.
A requirement to hide the tool’s output from users.

practiceQuestions.rationale: FDA GMLP addresses the total product lifecycle, while NIST frames risk management as ongoing. A governed deployment plan needs local testing and monitoring rather than a one-time vendor claim.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is accurate about the Emory Imaging Informatics Fellowship described by Emory?

options.text: It is a stand-alone imaging-informatics programme with no clinical training.
It is a two-year ACGME Clinical Informatics fellowship that independently establishes ABPM eligibility.
It is a one-year hybrid fellowship with equal informatics and clinical-subspecialty effort; applicants must be accepted by both programmes.
It is the same as the resident-only I3T track.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Emory describes a one-year 50/50 hybrid and joint acceptance. Its related I3T is an Emory resident track, not the fellowship. Emory does not state on the fellowship page that it is a 24-month ACGME Clinical Informatics fellowship.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the correct certification statement for “Imaging Informatics Fellowship” as this course title is used?

options.text: It is an ABR subspecialty certificate listed alongside Nuclear Radiology.
The fellowship itself automatically awards CIIP.
It names an institutional fellowship; ABMS’s ABR list does not show a separate Imaging Informatics subspecialty certificate.
It creates state medical licensure.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABMS lists ABR primary certificates and subspecialties but not Imaging Informatics. ABII separately administers the CIIP designation under its own qualification process. Neither this course nor the fellowship page is a licensure pathway.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about a 36-hour lecture ledger is valid for this independent course?

options.text: Recorded webinar duration is equivalent to supervised clinical rotation time.
A planned original clip can be counted before it is rendered and published.
Each public recording may be counted once by unique video ID; documented foundation time must remain separate from imaging-informatics-specific time.
Repeated playlists may be counted again for each unit.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ledger deduplicates public video IDs and separates foundation from specialty-focused time. Rotations, planned clips, and repeat views are not verified external lecture hours.

title: Interventional Neuroradiology Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (independent educational analogue; one named Emory clinical fellowship; interventional-neurology certification is a distinct credential)-aligned independent study

prerequisites.level: Advanced physician self-study analogue for learners who have completed the relevant residency/fellowship foundations; also usable as a non-credentialing overview by other health professionals.
prerequisites.recommended: Cerebrovascular anatomy, stroke pathophysiology, CT/CTA and MR basics, basic evidence appraisal, and knowledge of consent/safety principles.
prerequisites.notRequiredForAccess: No patient care, image acquisition, invasive access, device handling, or clinical observation is authorized by access to this material.
prerequisites.clinicalRestrictions: No real patient care, patient-specific diagnosis or treatment recommendation, supervised case volume, technical/procedural authorization, or licensure is provided.

objectives: Map neurovascular anatomy and major variants relevant to diagnostic interpretation.
Interpret guideline and board-blueprint domains in their correct date, scope, evidence grade and eligibility context.
Reason through neurointerventional case selection, imaging, alternatives, risk, complications and uncertainty at an educational level.
Distinguish Emory CAST-approved CV/INR training, ACGME neuroendovascular accreditation, UCNS Interventional Neurology certification and ABR neuroradiology certification.
Communicate case reasoning safely without converting general evidence into patient-specific orders or procedural instruction.

units.title: Cerebrovascular anatomy and angiographic road maps
objectives: Trace internal and external carotid, vertebrobasilar, spinal arterial, venous, and key collateral pathways relevant to safe interpretation.
Recognize segmental variants and clinically consequential anastomoses on angiographic projections.
Build a structured diagnostic angiography interpretation from indication through conclusion.
units.casePractice: Create a labeled projection-by-projection anatomy map from the linked public angiogram; write a non-procedural diagnostic report.

units.title: Imaging selection, perfusion, radiation and contrast
objectives: Compare CT/CTA, CTP, MRI/MRA and catheter angiography by the question asked, limitations, and urgency.
Explain how acquisition, motion, timing and post-processing can affect perfusion maps and selection.
Apply ALARA concepts and recognize contrast, radiation, and access tradeoffs without giving patient-specific orders.
units.casePractice: Prepare a modality comparison and safety checklist; distinguish source observations from automated software outputs.

units.title: Acute ischemic stroke: systems, eligibility and imaging selection
objectives: Summarize the current 2026 AHA/ASA AIS guidance relevant to EVT, IV thrombolysis, large ischemic cores, basilar occlusion and pediatric patients.
Interpret the LVO problem in context: time, deficit, imaging, premorbid status, transfer logistics and competing risks.
State why clinical decisions require the responsible multidisciplinary team and current local protocol.
boardDomains: UCNS I.C.1, II.D; 2026 AHA/ASA AIS guideline domains
units.casePractice: Complete a fictional case timeline and evidence matrix using the 2026 guideline; no treatment recommendation for a real patient.

units.title: Thrombectomy reasoning and procedural concepts
objectives: Describe the conceptual differences among stent-retriever and aspiration approaches, emphasizing goals and decision points rather than technical instruction.
Reason through common anatomic, access, clot and reperfusion tradeoffs using simulated cases.
Recognize that reperfusion grade, disability outcomes and complications are distinct measures.
units.casePractice: Write a case conference summary identifying unknowns, alternatives and evidence gaps; no device or procedural selection for a real patient.

units.title: Access, diagnostic catheterization, anesthesia and suite safety
objectives: Explain preprocedure planning, informed consent elements, team brief, sterile systems, access options and postprocedure monitoring at a conceptual level.
Compare femoral and radial access considerations without implying a universal preferred route.
Recognize contrast reactions, access complications, radiation hazards and anesthesia-related tradeoffs.
units.casePractice: Draft a team-based preprocedure safety briefing and postprocedure observation checklist for a fictional case.

units.title: Neurointerventional pharmacology and antithrombotic reasoning
objectives: Identify major antiplatelet, anticoagulant, thrombolytic, reversal and vasodilator classes on the UCNS outline.
Interpret the 2023 SNIS antithrombotic recommendations while noting evidence grades, indication-specific variation and local protocol.
Explain how thrombosis, bleeding, stent/device, comorbidity and procedure timing enter risk-benefit analysis.
units.casePractice: Create a decision tree of questions—not a dosing protocol—covering indication, bleeding/thrombotic risk, consultation and monitoring.

units.title: Intracranial aneurysms and aneurysmal SAH
objectives: Summarize aneurysm morphology, rupture context, treatment alternatives and multidisciplinary decision factors.
Apply the 2023 AHA/ASA aSAH guideline themes: prompt specialist evaluation, source securing, DCI prevention/monitoring and follow-up imaging.
Compare coiling, adjunctive techniques, flow diversion and intrasaccular therapy as categories; no procedural how-to.
units.casePractice: Analyze linked public case without copying images; produce a multidisciplinary case conference note with uncertainty and follow-up questions.

units.title: Brain AVMs, dural AV fistulae and cavernous-carotid fistulae
objectives: Distinguish parenchymal AVM from dural arteriovenous shunt and direct/indirect carotid-cavernous fistula.
Use venous drainage, hemorrhage presentation, natural-history considerations and multidisciplinary alternatives in risk framing.
Compare embolization as part of multimodality care, not a stand-alone presumed solution.
units.casePractice: Classify fictional shunt vignettes and identify which missing angiographic features prevent a confident management discussion.

units.title: Cervical carotid/vertebral disease, dissection and intracranial stenosis
objectives: Compare extracranial carotid/vertebral lesions, dissection, traumatic injury and intracranial atherosclerotic disease.
Separate medical therapy and revascularization questions and distinguish elective from emergent contexts.
Review stenting/angioplasty as options with indication, antiplatelet and embolic-risk constraints.
units.casePractice: Build a comparative evidence grid separating disease state, clinical goal, evidence, uncertainty and potential alternatives.

units.title: Venous, spinal and less common neurovascular conditions
objectives: Recognize cerebral venous sinus thrombosis and distinguish first-line anticoagulation from selected endovascular rescue discussion.
Map spinal vascular anatomy and differential diagnosis at a conceptual level.
Identify where evidence is sparse and where disease-specific multidisciplinary evaluation is essential.
units.casePractice: Write a one-page uncertainty appraisal for a fictional CVST or spinal vascular case; avoid prescriptive procedural steps.

units.title: Complications, rescue concepts, quality and patient safety
objectives: Recognize hemorrhage, vessel perforation, embolic events, access hematoma, dissection, contrast reaction, coagulopathy and radiation risks.
Organize response reasoning around early recognition, escalation, communication and local emergency protocols.
Use debriefing, morbidity and mortality, incident learning and quality measures without inventing institutional benchmarks.
boardDomains: UCNS II.Q; ACGME Neuroendovascular Intervention competencies
units.casePractice: Conduct a tabletop failure-mode analysis and structured debrief of a wholly fictional complication scenario.

units.title: Evidence appraisal, certification distinctions and integrated board review
objectives: Map study content to the published UCNS 50/50 content outline and distinguish it from ABR neuroradiology or neurosurgical certification.
Evaluate trial/guideline applicability, study design, patient-centered outcomes, conflicts and date currency.
Present an integrated case conference with alternatives, uncertainty and explicit limits on self-study competence.
boardDomains: UCNS I-II; ABR neuroradiology scope; ACGME educational and safety requirements
units.casePractice: Complete the capstone board-domain map and oral-style case discussion; rubric scores reasoning, evidence use and limitations, not procedural competence.

components.task: Create a dated evidence brief for acute ischemic stroke, aneurysmal SAH, an AV shunt, and one venous/cervical/spinal case using public sources and linked-only images.
components.deliverable: Four 1–2 page briefs plus one integrated multidisciplinary conference summary. Cases may be source-linked clinical examples or labeled fictional educational vignettes; no copied patient record or image.

components.task: Make an accreditation/certification matrix comparing Emory CV/INR, ACGME Neuroendovascular Intervention, UCNS Interventional Neurology and ABR Neuroradiology.
components.deliverable: One-page comparison with source, date, exact scope, and unknowns.
A fictional failure-mode map and structured debrief, with escalation roles but no procedure or drug instructions.

assessment.formative: Unit case notes, short-answer retrieval checks and evidence matrices. Faculty grading is not offered.
assessment.summative: Ten original multiple-choice items plus a written capstone case conference and blueprint mapping.
assessment.passingStandard: No validated cut score is claimed; self-assessment only. Questions are original educational items, not official exam content. No prediction of board passage.

unitMap.text: Cerebrovascular anatomy and angiographic road maps
Imaging selection, perfusion, radiation and contrast
Acute ischemic stroke: systems, eligibility and imaging selection
Thrombectomy reasoning and procedural concepts
Access, diagnostic catheterization, anesthesia and suite safety
Neurointerventional pharmacology and antithrombotic reasoning
Intracranial aneurysms and aneurysmal SAH
Brain AVMs, dural AV fistulae and cavernous-carotid fistulae
Cervical carotid/vertebral disease, dissection and intracranial stenosis
Venous, spinal and less common neurovascular conditions
Complications, rescue concepts, quality and patient safety
Evidence appraisal, certification distinctions and integrated board review

topicGaps: The 14 verified recordings provide 13.15 total observed hours (9.49 specialty-specific and 3.66 foundational), leaving 22.85 hours below the 36-hour target. Authored scripts remain unrecorded and add zero verified hours.

Unit 6 has no verified recording focused on neurointerventional antithrombotic pharmacology, HIT, reversal concepts, or evidence-graded decision context. SNIS article remains the source reading; it is not counted as a video.

Unit 9 has only limited recorded coverage of cervical disease: the thrombectomy case lecture mentions tandem lesions/dissections and anatomy lectures cover vessels, but no accessible, duration-verified lecture on elective carotid/vertebral disease was confirmed. The apparent WSA video listing was excluded because its direct URL returned an advertisement rather than the lecture.
Unit 10 has verified cerebral venous sinus thrombosis teaching, but no verified recording on spinal vascular lesions/angiography, traumatic vascular injury, or provocative testing.
Unit 11 gains radiation safety and chronic subdural hematoma material, but there is no dedicated verified lecture on the full complication/rescue, quality-improvement and institutional-safety domain.

Unit 12 has no verified recorded lecture devoted to evidence appraisal, eligibility/certification distinctions, or board-domain integration. UCNS outline is an examination content map only, not instruction or a second board for this fellowship.

No verified recordings were found for several UCNS outline subdomains: tumor embolization, vasospasm intervention, Wada/balloon test occlusion, and detailed spinal angiography. Do not infer coverage from the published blueprint or from adjacent topics.

Multiple specialist videos contain detailed procedure or patient-case discussions. They are external conceptual resources only; watch-page access does not grant rights to copy/rehost clinical images, and self-study does not qualify anyone to perform procedures.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.boardStatus: No universal separate examination specifically titled “Interventional Neuroradiology” was identified in the official board sources checked; that is not proof that no other local or non-US credential exists. There is not one uniform board pathway for all physicians using “interventional neuroradiology/neurointervention.” UCNS offers a distinct Interventional Neurology subspecialty examination with its own eligibility pathways; ABR offers a separate Neuroradiology subspecialty exam for eligible radiologists. Emory describes this fellowship as CAST-approved; CAST approval is not itself a separate physician board exam. ACGME Neuroendovascular Intervention program requirements are a separate accreditation framework. This course is not accredited and conveys no board eligibility.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: UCNS eligibility (criteria updated 2025-12-11) requires primary certification in neurology, neurological surgery, or radiology (or specified equivalents), current active unrestricted licensure in an applicable jurisdiction, and one of the published pathways; accredited-fellowship pathway requires a UCNS-accredited 24+ month fellowship, but other pathways exist. Do not assume Emory CAST approval automatically equals UCNS accreditation or confers UCNS eligibility. ABR neuroradiology eligibility is a distinct radiology route. Confirm current requirements with each board and program.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The source packet names only Emory’s clinical physician CV/INR fellowship. No Harvard or Johns Hopkins offering is claimed for this item. The scope preserves Emory’s exact “Cerebrovascular/Interventional Neuroradiology” name and separately notes general SNIS multi-specialty pathways, UCNS Interventional Neurology certification, CAST approval, and ACGME Neuroendovascular Intervention. WSO International Neurointerventional Fellowship is a separate international supplement, not an Emory institutional variant or US physician-board pathway. This is a clinical physician fellowship with an embedded research component, not a research-only postdoctoral position or a non-physician training track; none is substituted for the packet’s physician fellowship.
sourceCaveats: No human clinical review has been performed.
This is not Harvard/Johns Hopkins/Emory-affiliated, accredited, or supervised education. The source packet’s Emory program is the only institutional variant in this specialty packet.

Program-page scope and institution facts are distinguished from accreditor requirements, board eligibility and examination blueprint. Public pages may change; recheck with institutions, ACGME, UCNS, ABR, CAST and SNIS.

The ACGME 2026 Neuroendovascular Intervention requirements are treated as a separate framework. Emory’s public page identifies CAST approval; program-specific ACGME status is not established by the evidence checked here.

The UCNS exam is Interventional Neurology, a real separate subspecialty certification examination, but not a universal board exam for all interventional neuroradiology/neuroendovascular physicians. ABR neuroradiology is also a separate certification, not interventional neuroradiology certification.

The requested 36 hours are a video curriculum target, not a claim of equivalent clinical training. Only accessible free recordings with observed runtime can count; none met that bar in this research pass.
Case links are external. De-identification is not independently audited in this course. No patient images, medical records, protected media or proprietary exam questions are copied or redistributed.
No diagnosis, case-volume minimum, individual eligibility determination, guaranteed board passage or procedural competence is stated.

No universal US board examination specifically titled Interventional Neuroradiology was identified in the official sources checked; UCNS Interventional Neurology and ABR Neuroradiology exams are separate credentials. This is a qualified finding, not an exhaustive global credential survey.

topicGaps: The 14 verified recordings provide 13.15 total observed hours (9.49 specialty-specific and 3.66 foundational), leaving 22.85 hours below the 36-hour target. Authored scripts remain unrecorded and add zero verified hours.

Unit 6 has no verified recording focused on neurointerventional antithrombotic pharmacology, HIT, reversal concepts, or evidence-graded decision context. SNIS article remains the source reading; it is not counted as a video.

Unit 9 has only limited recorded coverage of cervical disease: the thrombectomy case lecture mentions tandem lesions/dissections and anatomy lectures cover vessels, but no accessible, duration-verified lecture on elective carotid/vertebral disease was confirmed. The apparent WSA video listing was excluded because its direct URL returned an advertisement rather than the lecture.
Unit 10 has verified cerebral venous sinus thrombosis teaching, but no verified recording on spinal vascular lesions/angiography, traumatic vascular injury, or provocative testing.
Unit 11 gains radiation safety and chronic subdural hematoma material, but there is no dedicated verified lecture on the full complication/rescue, quality-improvement and institutional-safety domain.

Unit 12 has no verified recorded lecture devoted to evidence appraisal, eligibility/certification distinctions, or board-domain integration. UCNS outline is an examination content map only, not instruction or a second board for this fellowship.

No verified recordings were found for several UCNS outline subdomains: tumor embolization, vasospasm intervention, Wada/balloon test occlusion, and detailed spinal angiography. Do not infer coverage from the published blueprint or from adjacent topics.

Multiple specialist videos contain detailed procedure or patient-case discussions. They are external conceptual resources only; watch-page access does not grant rights to copy/rehost clinical images, and self-study does not qualify anyone to perform procedures.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A course learner sees a current AHA/ASA summary stating that EVT is recommended for selected adults with basilar artery occlusion presenting within 24 hours and NIHSS at least 10. What is the safest interpretation for this independent curriculum?

options.text: This threshold is a universal independent order to proceed with EVT.
It is a guideline-level selection statement that must be applied by the responsible stroke team to the actual patient and current full guideline/local protocol.
It proves all posterior circulation occlusions benefit equally.
It replaces standard clinical imaging.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2026 guideline summary identifies this group for a strong EVT recommendation, but an educational summary is not a stand-alone patient order and does not remove individual assessment, contraindications, or local protocols.

practiceQuestions.stem: The same 2026 AHA/ASA summary addresses large ischemic-core stroke. Which statement is best supported?

options.text: Large core is an automatic exclusion from EVT.
Recent evidence supports EVT for some patients previously considered ineligible because of larger cores; individual selection still matters.
The guideline says core volume alone determines treatment.
Any large infarct must be treated with thrombectomy.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline notes evidence supporting expanded EVT to some larger-core populations, not a categorical rule for all patients.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has aneurysmal SAH and a suspected ruptured aneurysm. Which 2023 guideline concept is accurate?

options.text: Delay all source evaluation until vasospasm is evident.
Prompt specialist evaluation and treatment of the ruptured aneurysm, preferably within 24 hours, is recommended when feasible; modality choice is individualized by experts.
Complete obliteration is never a goal.
Hypervolemia should routinely be induced to prevent delayed cerebral ischemia.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AHA/ASA recommends prompt evaluation and treatment, preferably within 24 hours, with treatment strategy balancing patient and aneurysm characteristics. Routine hypervolemia is not recommended.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best reflects the SNIS 2023 guidance regarding patients with cerebral venous sinus thrombosis?

options.text: Endovascular therapy is universal first-line treatment.
Heparin anticoagulation is front-line therapy; endovascular therapy may be considered, particularly with clinical deterioration despite medical therapy.
All anticoagulation is prohibited.
No specialist review is necessary.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline explicitly describes heparin anticoagulation as front-line and endovascular therapy as a possible consideration particularly when clinical deterioration occurs despite medical treatment.

practiceQuestions.stem: An unruptured brain AVM patient uses an antithrombotic for another established disease. What does the 2023 SNIS guideline state?

options.text: Always stop the antithrombotic solely because of the AVM.
There is no indication to change antiplatelet or anticoagulant management instituted for another disease solely due to an unruptured AVM, per that recommendation.
Start dual antiplatelet therapy for every AVM.
The guideline requires endovascular AVM treatment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: SNIS recommendation 7 says there is no indication to change antiplatelet or anticoagulant management instituted for another disease in patients with unruptured brain AVMs. Real decisions remain individualized.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is the most accurate description of the UCNS Interventional Neurology examination blueprint?

options.text: All questions are neurovascular disease states.
Two primary content areas, neurovascular disease states/conditions and neurointerventional procedures/techniques, each comprise 50%.
It is an ABR neuroradiology exam.
It is an ACGME program accreditation decision.

practiceQuestions.rationale: UCNS publishes a 200-question outline with two equally weighted domains. It is a distinct UCNS subspecialty examination, not the ABR neuroradiology exam or ACGME accreditation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which distinction about the Emory CV/INR fellowship is supported by the program page?

options.text: It is described as a one-year ACGME diagnostic neuroradiology fellowship.
Emory describes a CAST-approved two-year CV/INR fellowship accepting graduates from neurosurgery, stroke/neuro-ICU trained neurology, or neuroradiology-trained radiology.
It is a non-physician technologist course.
It guarantees all graduates a separate neurointerventional board certificate.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official Emory page explicitly describes its program as a CAST-approved two-year fellowship and lists those physician backgrounds. It does not claim an independent board certificate.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner encounters an ACGME program-requirement PDF titled Neuroendovascular Intervention while studying Emory’s CV/INR page. What is the correct inference?

options.text: Every CAST-approved program is automatically ACGME-accredited.
The ACGME requirement is a separate accreditation standard; do not assume Emory’s publicly identified CAST-approved program is ACGME-accredited unless a program-specific source confirms that.
The two labels must mean exactly the same thing.
Any ACGME requirement establishes UCNS certification eligibility for every applicant.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Accreditation regimes and institutional descriptions must not be collapsed. Emory’s page says CAST-approved; the ACGME document has its own requirements.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with recent coronary stenting is considered for endovascular aneurysm treatment. Which statement matches the SNIS antithrombotic update?

options.text: DAPT is recommended for neurointerventional aneurysm treatment in a patient with cardiac stents placed within the prior 6–12 months.
All antithrombotic agents should be stopped in all cases.
The guidance says medications never affect device-associated thrombotic risk.
A self-study module can prescribe the individual regimen.

options.text: Early enteral nimodipine is beneficial; routine statin and IV magnesium use are not recommended.
Routine prophylactic hypervolemia is recommended.
Follow-up cerebrovascular imaging is unnecessary.
Antifibrinolytic therapy routinely improves functional outcomes.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The summary states early enteral nimodipine is beneficial, routine statin and IV magnesium are not recommended, and prophylactic hemodynamic augmentation/hypervolemia should not be performed.

title: Medical Physics Imaging Residency
level: Supplementary non-physician medical-physics residency-aligned independent study

prerequisites.level: Graduate-level independent study for learners with physics and quantitative preparation; not entry-level clinical training.
knowledge: Calculus, algebra, probability/statistics and basic electromagnetism
Introductory anatomy/physiology and radiation interactions; use OpenStax and IAEA handbooks to remediate
prerequisites.requiredDisclosure: No access to supervised clinical measurements, systems, protected health information or patient records is provided.

objectives: Explain core diagnostic-imaging physics, image quality and dose indices.
Describe modality-specific system evaluation topics across Emory’s publicly named rotation domains.
Map course topics cautiously to ABR public examination and clinical-training descriptions without implying examination readiness.
Critically appraise technical evidence, uncertainty, current regulation, image-data rights and AI validation claims.
Communicate limits and escalate safety issues through qualified local physicists and facility processes.

units.title: Physics foundations, image quality, and professional role
objectives: Relate signal, noise, spatial resolution, contrast, and task-based image quality.
Distinguish medical physicist responsibilities from physician interpretation and technologist operation.
Explain quality culture and risk communication.
topics: Image formation overview; image quality; professional conduct; QA/QC vocabulary; patient-centred communication.
units.boardDomains: Part 1 General/Clinical foundations; Part 2 diagnostic practice context
casePractice: Video 3-question concept check; short calculation on SNR/resolution tradeoff.
units.assessment: Create a one-page modality-agnostic QA problem statement. Rubric: physics correctness 40%, appropriate role/scope 25%, evidence 20%, clarity 15%.

units.title: Radiography systems and image acquisition
objectives: Trace x-ray generation, beam quality, detector conversion, and image processing.
Interpret exposure indicators and identify saturation/noise tradeoffs without assuming a single vendor scale.
Describe acceptance/performance evaluation questions for radiography.
topics: Tube output and filtration; detector response; CR/DR; exposure index; spatial resolution; image artifacts.
units.boardDomains: Part 1 General; Part 2 general-purpose radiography and storage-phosphor/digital-detector evaluation
casePractice: Compare two supplied exposure-indicator scenarios; link the x-ray tube lecture and IAEA chapters.
units.assessment: Write a radiography evaluation plan. Rubric: measurement logic 35%, artifact differential 25%, safety 20%, limits 20%.

units.title: Fluoroscopy and interventional imaging
objectives: Explain pulsed fluoroscopy, ABC, dose-rate, geometry, and displayed dose indices.
Describe physicist participation in interventional equipment evaluation and dose optimization.
Differentiate patient skin-dose concern from cumulative reference-point indicators.
topics: Automatic brightness control; pulse rate; geometry; dose indices; staff protection; dose-management review.
units.boardDomains: Part 2 fluoroscopy/interventional x-ray evaluation and shielding design
casePractice: Dose-index interpretation worksheet using fictional values, with uncertainty statement.
units.assessment: Submit a protocol optimization memo. Rubric: correct indices 30%, geometry reasoning 25%, protection 25%, evidence/limits 20%.

units.title: Acceptance testing, quality control, and performance monitoring
objectives: Build a risk-informed QC and acceptance-testing framework.
Separate commissioning, acceptance, routine QC, constancy checks, and regulatory survey.
Explain why a retired guidance document cannot substitute for current standards or local policy.
topics: Test design; baselines; tolerances; trending; remote QC; dynamic systems; corrective action.
units.boardDomains: Part 2 evaluation of diagnostic workstations, modalities and clinical equipment; Part 1 general physics
casePractice: Draft a sample QC matrix with test, frequency rationale, failure escalation; use public IOMP QC talks.
units.assessment: QC program critique. Rubric: test relevance 30%, baseline/trending 25%, escalation 25%, currency/sourcing 20%.

units.title: Mammography and breast imaging physics
objectives: Explain mammographic detector, compression, AEC, dose and image-quality tradeoffs.
Summarize annual physicist survey role under MQSA and distinguish it from full facility certification.
Discuss stereotactic biopsy system evaluation at a conceptual level.
topics: Screen-film history; digital mammography; tomosynthesis; dose; phantom/image quality; MQSA; biopsy guidance.
units.boardDomains: Part 2 mammography annual system evaluation and stereotactic breast biopsy system performance evaluation
casePractice: Use virtual breast imaging trial lecture; answer a fictional phantom-result interpretation exercise.
units.assessment: Regulatory comparison memo. Rubric: distinguish facility/personnel rules 30%, physics reasoning 30%, correct limits 20%, citations 20%.

units.title: Computed tomography and dosimetry
objectives: Explain CT acquisition parameters and scanner performance metrics.
Calculate and interpret CTDIvol/DLP with explicit limitations; avoid treating either as patient-specific absorbed dose.
Describe CT performance evaluation and dose optimization pathways.
topics: Helical CT; pitch; collimation; CTDIvol; DLP; size-specific dose estimate concepts; image noise; reconstruction; QC.
units.boardDomains: Part 2 CT system performance evaluation; shielding design for CT scanner
casePractice: Solve fictional CTDIvol/DLP and protocol tradeoff questions; critique what dose index cannot infer.
units.assessment: CT optimization brief. Rubric: units/calculations 30%, limitations 30%, image quality 20%, safety communication 20%.

units.title: MRI physics, image quality, and safety
objectives: Relate Larmor frequency, gradients, k-space sampling and acquisition to image contrast/resolution.
Identify static field, gradient, RF, implant, projectile, heating, and acoustic safety hazards.
Use the current ACR manual as a reference while deferring operational clearance to local MR safety procedures.
topics: Spin echo/gradient echo concepts; frequency encoding; sampling; SNR; artifacts; safety zones; implants and device screening.
units.boardDomains: Part 2 MRI system performance evaluation and MR safety evaluation
casePractice: Draw a k-space sampling explanation; complete fictional hazard triage with explicit escalation.
units.assessment: MR safety scenario analysis. Rubric: hazard recognition 35%, escalation 30%, physics 20%, scope discipline 15%.

units.title: Ultrasound and bone mineral measurement: gap module
objectives: Explain pulse-echo, attenuation, transducer frequency, axial/lateral resolution and Doppler basics.
Name performance evaluation questions for diagnostic ultrasound and bone mineral analyzers.
Recognize this area has no verified video in the curated evidence set.
topics: Acoustic impedance; pulse-echo; beamforming; Doppler; image artifacts; phantom QA; bone mineral analyzer.
units.boardDomains: Part 2 ultrasound system performance evaluation; bone mineral analyzer evaluation
casePractice: Use a provided non-patient phantom diagram and write a conceptual QC checklist; do not perform equipment testing.
units.assessment: Gap worksheet. Rubric: acoustic concepts 35%, test rationale 30%, safety/scope 20%, clear gap identification 15%.

units.title: Imaging informatics, display, and AI governance
objectives: Trace an image from acquisition to archive using DICOM objects and services.
Explain modality-worklist, storage, display calibration, PACS/RIS interoperability, privacy and cybersecurity basics.
Evaluate an imaging-AI performance claim for validation population, task, bias, drift, and workflow fit.
topics: DICOM information objects; transfer syntax; query/retrieve; DICOMweb; grayscale display; PACS; AI oversight; data governance.
units.boardDomains: Part 2 diagnostic workstation evaluation; ABR Part 1 ethics/professionalism
casePractice: Map a fictional study workflow and critique a fictional AI claim card; no clinical deployment decisions.
units.assessment: Workflow diagram plus AI evidence appraisal. Rubric: standards fidelity 30%, security/privacy 25%, validation 25%, scope 20%.

units.title: Nuclear medicine instrumentation, quantification, and safety
objectives: Explain scintillation camera, SPECT and PET image formation and major corrections.
Describe radionuclide imaging performance evaluation and dose calibrator/well counter checks at a conceptual level.
Distinguish medical physics performance evaluation from diagnostic interpretation and therapy decisions.
topics: Gamma camera; collimator; SPECT reconstruction; PET coincidence; attenuation/scatter/random corrections; quantification; radiation protection; hybrid CT.
units.boardDomains: Part 2 nuclear medical physics is a separate ABR specialty; these topics are relevant supplement, not proof of eligibility for it.
casePractice: Compare fictional PET/SPECT correction chains; state what missing data prevent interpreting patient dose or a scan.
units.assessment: Correction-chain diagram and short concept quiz. Rubric: modality accuracy 35%, correction logic 25%, safety 20%, limits 20%.

units.title: Radiation protection, regulation, and risk communication
objectives: Differentiate stochastic-risk model assumptions, dose quantities, and exposure indicators.
Explain justification/optimization and patient/staff protection at a high level without giving individual treatment advice.
Identify when pregnancy, repeat imaging, shielding, or an incident requires local expert review and current guidance.
topics: Dose quantities; diagnostic reference levels; justification; optimization; staff protection; pregnancy; shielding; incident response; regulations.
units.boardDomains: Part 1 clinical/radiobiology; Part 2 shielding design and facility safety duties
casePractice: Risk-communication rewrite exercise; explain why a single numerical threshold is not an individual patient safety guarantee.
units.assessment: Communication rubric: factual accuracy 35%, uncertainty 25%, actionability/escalation 25%, empathy/plain language 15%.

units.title: Integrated evaluation, research methods, and board map
objectives: Integrate equipment, image quality, dose, safety, QA and informatics reasoning in a fictional cross-modality scenario.
Design a literature-supported research question, endpoints, uncertainty and limitations.
Map learning only to published ABR exam/training descriptions, not claim equivalence to accredited competency or passing.
topics: Acceptance/evaluation planning; uncertainty; phantom versus patient data; protocol change management; AI/QA; research ethics; board blueprint limitations.
units.boardDomains: ABR Part 1 General/Clinical and Part 2 Diagnostic Medical Physics; published clinical training evaluation list
casePractice: Capstone uses a fictional multi-modality QC incident, selected public LIDC-IDRI data only under terms, or phantoms. No patient records/images copied or rehosted.
units.assessment: Capstone rubric: sound physics 25%, safety/regulatory reasoning 25%, evidence/uncertainty 20%, data stewardship 15%, scope and communication 15%.

assignment.name: Cross-modality performance evaluation portfolio (fictional)
components: One modality evaluation plan (select radiography, CT, MRI, mammography, fluoro or nuclear imaging)
One fictional QC trend and failure escalation memo
One final reflection mapping learning to ABR public domains and naming gaps
assignment.grading: Self-study formative portfolio; no competency determination, accreditation, board prediction or clinical authorization.

assessment.formative: Low-stakes unit quizzes, calculation exercises using fictional values, and case-resource literacy prompts.
assessment.summative: 10 original educational questions and the portfolio above.
assessment.passRule: Suggested self-check only: 80% on question set plus complete rubric feedback. Not validated and not a predictor of ABR outcome.
assessment.rubric: Assessment emphasizes physics explanation, correct quantity/units, method, evidence currency, uncertainty and escalation.

studyHours.plan: Approximately 86 hours: 36.15 hours verified recorded media, 24 hours textbook/standard reading, 16 hours written exercises, 8 hours portfolio and review, 1.85 hours quiz/reflection. This is a self-study plan, not a residency duration or clinical practice equivalence.

mapping.name: Medical Physics Imaging Residency
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page describes a 24-month CAMPEP-accredited imaging-physics residency; rotations: general radiography, fluoroscopy/interventional radiography, mammography, CT, MRI, nuclear medicine, radiology informatics, dosimetry/radiation safety and ultrasound. Includes seminars, research and advanced topics. This is medical physics, not physician training. Separate Emory Nuclear Medicine Training Program is listed for 12 months and explicitly not currently accepting applicants; no public evidence reviewed here establishes that it is a combined 2+1 track with this 24-month imaging program. Preserve separate identities.

officialProgrammes.name: Medical Physics Imaging Residency
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page describes a 24-month CAMPEP-accredited imaging-physics residency; rotations: general radiography, fluoroscopy/interventional radiography, mammography, CT, MRI, nuclear medicine, radiology informatics, dosimetry/radiation safety and ultrasound. Includes seminars, research and advanced topics. This is medical physics, not physician training. Separate Emory Nuclear Medicine Training Program is listed for 12 months and explicitly not currently accepting applicants; no public evidence reviewed here establishes that it is a combined 2+1 track with this 24-month imaging program. Preserve separate identities.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The input packet names one exact institutional variant: Emory University School of Medicine — Medical Physics Imaging Residency. CAMPEP directory (last updated 2026-09-28) separately lists Emory in its Imaging section and marks Emory with a nuclear-medicine-physics option; this directory marker is not proof that two listed Emory offerings form one combined 2+1 program. Emory also advertises a separate Nuclear Medicine Training Program and says it is not accepting applicants this cycle. No Harvard or Johns Hopkins physician specialty is being inferred or added to this one-item track. It is an institutional training program category for non-physician medical physicists, not a generic physician residency, not a research-only postdoc, and not a combined program on evidence reviewed.
sourceCaveats: Emory page and brochure are public descriptions, not its complete internal didactic curriculum or rotation checklist; public source text gives only a high-level schedule.
CAMPEP directory and Emory pages establish programme categorization/accreditation claims, not an individual trainee’s eligibility or outcome.
ABR examination guidance is current as checked 2026-10-07. Recheck board standards, exam dates and eligibility before use; no promise of passing.
AAPM Report 74 is explicitly inactive and is included only as historical reading, not present-day protocol.
Public YouTube metadata records observed runtime and access status on 2026-10-07; future availability may change. Link to videos only and do not infer re-use or embedding rights.
Human clinical review is not performed. No real-patient images, records, diagnoses, dose prescriptions or invented clinical volumes are supplied.

practiceQuestions.stem: A detector exposure indicator rises after a protocol change, but image appearance is window/level normalized. Which conclusion is best?

options.text: Higher displayed signal proves the exam dose increased by the same ratio.
The indicator is a vendor/system-specific exposure-related quantity; review its definition, acquisition conditions and dose metrics before concluding.
The image is necessarily overexposed and unusable.
The technologist should change technique without physicist review.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Exposure indicators are not interchangeable with patient dose and may depend on vendor/calibration; assess the system and acquisition context.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fluoroscopy procedure shows a high cumulative reference-point air kerma. What is the best first physics interpretation?

options.text: It equals the patient skin dose exactly.
It is an indicator requiring contextual review of geometry, backscatter, table/pad attenuation and dose distribution; it is not a direct skin-dose map.
It is the same as effective dose.
It determines a radiation injury diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Displayed fluoroscopy dose indices are operational quantities and require qualified interpretation; they do not alone map the skin-dose distribution.

practiceQuestions.stem: A CT dose report lists CTDIvol and DLP. Which statement is correct?

options.text: CTDIvol is an exact individualized organ dose.
DLP is CTDIvol multiplied by scan length; both are scanner output descriptors and not exact patient-specific absorbed dose.
DLP equals effective dose for all patients.
CTDIvol includes all prior scans for that person.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CTDIvol and DLP are standardized scanner output indices; patient size, scan range and protocol affect dose interpretation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Under MQSA, which statement most accurately describes the physicist role?

options.text: The physicist alone certifies the mammography facility.
A medical physicist or supervised physicist conducts an annual survey as part of broader facility requirements; facility certification/accreditation involve separate requirements.
MQSA applies only to image interpretation.
Annual survey removes all other QA obligations.

practiceQuestions.rationale: FDA describes annual physicist survey plus facility certification, accreditation, image review and ongoing quality standards.

practiceQuestions.stem: A worker brings an unknown implant into the MR environment. Which is the safest response?

options.text: Assume it is safe if nonferromagnetic on a consumer label.
Pause entry and follow institutional MR safety screening/escalation; verify exact device and conditions with qualified MR safety staff.
Use a lower field strength without review.
Ask the patient to judge magnetic attraction.

practiceQuestions.rationale: MR device safety is device- and condition-specific and requires site procedures and trained review; an educational course does not authorize clearance.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which distinction between acceptance testing and routine QC is most appropriate?

options.text: They are synonyms.
Acceptance tests document delivered-system performance against requirements; routine QC tracks ongoing constancy/performance and triggers corrective action.
Routine QC is unnecessary after acceptance.
Only the manufacturer may perform either.

practiceQuestions.rationale: These are distinct quality-management stages; current standards and local policies determine tests and acceptance criteria.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which label correctly describes Emory’s 24-month Medical Physics Imaging Residency?

options.text: Physician diagnostic radiology residency.
CAMPEP-accredited non-physician medical physics residency with diagnostic imaging rotations.
ABR-certified fellowship that itself confers licensure.
A combined 2+1 diagnostic/nuclear medical physics residency.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Emory calls it a 24-month CAMPEP-accredited Medical Physics Imaging Residency. The official page lists nuclear medicine training separately and says not accepting applicants; no combined 2+1 claim is made.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is required to complete ABR medical physics certification under the ABR pathway described?

options.text: Part 1 only.
Parts 1, 2 and 3, after meeting board eligibility requirements.
Passing this self-study course.
Completing any 36 hours of lecture videos.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABR describes three exam parts and prerequisite/education/training criteria. A self-study course does not establish eligibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: A student wants to use a TCIA LIDC-IDRI image in a slide deck. What should they do?

options.text: Copy the image without attribution because it is de-identified.
Follow the collection license and TCIA use policy, provide required attribution, and avoid rehosting or redistribution beyond the license.
Remove the patient identifier and assume unrestricted use.
Use it as clinical ground truth without annotation limits.

practiceQuestions.rationale: TCIA lists CC BY 3.0 and required citation/policy obligations; de-identification is not permission to ignore license or terms.

practiceQuestions.stem: A research abstract reports high AI performance on a single public CT collection. What is the strongest immediate appraisal question?

options.text: Does it have the highest accuracy number?
Was the intended clinical task, external validation population, reference standard, calibration, subgroup performance and workflow impact assessed?
Was the data volume large?
Can the output be implemented without clinical validation?

practiceQuestions.rationale: A performance claim needs task-specific and external validation, reference standard and intended-use evaluation; a dataset score alone is insufficient.

title: Molecular Imaging Residency Program

objectives: Explain tracer biology and select imaging modalities conceptually for a clinical question.

Cross-calibration, normalization, daily QC and PET/CT fusion artifacts

10 CFR Part 35 and ABNM authorized-user relationship
Communication, pregnancy/lactation screening and local policy escalation

coveredTopics: Radiochemical identity, purity and quality control at physician level
Tracer affinity, metabolism, kinetics and target-to-background
Internal dosimetry assumptions and uncertainty; no clinical dose prescription

unitMap.text: General nuclear medicine procedures and reporting

Correlation with prior studies and cross-sectional imaging

PYP visual grade, SPECT confirmation, blood pool and AL exclusion

topicGaps: No verified full lecture sequence was located for adult myocardial perfusion, viability, inflammatory cardiac PET, comprehensive endocrine/GI/GU, pulmonary, adult neurology, broad pediatric nuclear medicine or systematic structured reporting. Added pediatric recordings are selected exemplars, not complete coverage.

Radiopharmaceutical handling/radiochemistry, radiation biology, full NRC/ABNM safety, broad instrument QC and safe operations remain materially underrepresented in verified video hours; viewing does not fulfill required supervised training or authorization.

Pediatric recordings now cover selected cardiac/lung perfusion, cortical renal/cystography, thyroid, bone, reflux/aspiration, neuroblastoma, PET/CT pitfalls and neurology. Age-specific normal variants, protocols, complete organ coverage and pediatric competence remain gaps.

Oncology recordings remain concentrated in thyroid and radionuclide therapy, now supplemented with one pediatric neuroblastoma overview and pediatric PET/CT pitfalls. No comprehensive adult tumor-by-modality course or full response-assessment sequence was located.

Current verified total is 13.3228 unique video hours (23 recordings; 4.1325 foundation and 9.1903 specialty). The verified residual gap to 36 h is 22.6772 h. Scripts/readings are not rendered or counted.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.boardStatus: The item name ‘Molecular Imaging’ is not a separate physician board specialty or examination. medical.programmeSourceScope: The packet’s exact Johns Hopkins directory listing is retained verbatim as the institutional variant, but current departmental programme information is titled Nuclear Medicine Residency and describes its ACGME-accredited NM program. The same page separately describes an ACGME-equivalent PET/CT clinical fellowship. Do not infer the directory label itself guarantees a dual board pathway. No Harvard-affiliated variant was included in this exact-item packet or independently verified here. No separate research-only or non-physician training program is counted as this clinical residency; nuclear medicine physics is foundational content, not a physician training credential.
sourceCaveats: The exact Hopkins directory record describes combined radiology and nuclear medicine training, while the current departmental page presents an ACGME-accredited Nuclear Medicine Residency and a separately described ACGME-equivalent PET/CT clinical fellowship. The pages do not establish that every holder of the directory-labelled slot is eligible for both ABNM and ABR certification.

The current ABNM blueprint is an examination-domain distribution, not a complete curriculum or guarantee of pass probability. Its certification-exam table lists Core 10%, Cardiovascular 16%, Oncology 34%, Therapy 10%, and the other named organ-system categories at 5% each; secondary classifications include Pediatrics and Correlative Imaging.

The ACGME 2026 Nuclear Medicine requirements specify a 36-month educational program. Hopkins describes duration as dependent on prior training. This educational study plan is not a residency and does not equate its video-hours floor to GME duration.

ABNM reports a separate secure certification exam. ABR Nuclear Radiology is a separate conditional subspecialty pathway requiring ABR specialty certification and specified nuclear-radiology/nuclear-medicine training. No standalone Molecular Imaging or PET/CT board examination was identified in sources checked.

The therapeutic product indication statements were checked against FDA notices dated 2025-03-28 and 2026-08-03. These notices are not substitutes for the current prescribing information, multidisciplinary review or patient-specific clinical judgment.
Interactive IAEA courses may require dynamic browser execution; stateless retrieval showed an entry page and an offline/reconnecting state for one module. No duration or completed media was inferred.

The lecture evidence reuses 14 public IAEA-channel video records already duration-checked in a neighboring nuclear-medicine evidence ledger; no other specialty file was edited. The ledger states that public Invidious metadata endpoints were used to observe runtime after direct YouTube extraction was rate-limited. This is duration evidence, not provider identity or guaranteed ongoing availability.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner is comparing the principal detector logic of PET and conventional SPECT. Which description is most accurate?

options.text: PET localizes paired annihilation photons in coincidence; SPECT generally uses a collimator to localize detected single photons.
SPECT requires positron annihilation; PET uses a mechanical collimator to identify single photons.
Both modalities directly measure tissue concentration without reconstruction.
Neither modality requires correction or reconstruction.

practiceQuestions.rationale: PET uses coincidence detection of annihilation-photon pairs, whereas conventional SPECT uses collimation for emitted photons. Both require image reconstruction and have correction/quality limits; the question tests modality fundamentals, not a complete physics syllabus.

practiceQuestions.stem: A cardiac PYP planar view appears to show uptake over the heart, but SPECT demonstrates that much of the activity is residual blood pool and there is no confident diffuse myocardial localization. What is the best educational interpretation principle?

options.text: Call ATTR whenever planar activity is visible over the heart.
Use the heart-to-contralateral ratio alone to override absent myocardial uptake on SPECT.
Do not diagnose ATTR from planar activity or a ratio alone; assess localization and technical/timing context and use appropriate clinical correlation.
Classify every blood-pool pattern as AL amyloidosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASNC guidance stresses SPECT localization to distinguish blood pool from myocardium, does not recommend one-hour planar-only imaging, and says PYP diagnosis cannot be made on H/CL ratio alone, especially without visually confirmed myocardial uptake on SPECT.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has visually confirmed diffuse myocardial PYP uptake with visual grade 2. Which important interpretive safeguard remains necessary before calling the pattern strongly suggestive of ATTR cardiac amyloidosis?

options.text: Exclude a monoclonal plasma-cell dyscrasia, including appropriate serum/urine testing, and interpret with clinical context.
Confirm the patient has a bone metastasis.
Treat grade 2 as pathognomonic regardless of laboratory findings.
Use a heart-to-contralateral ratio without reviewing SPECT.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASNC states that grade 2 or 3 is strongly suggestive of ATTR when AL amyloidosis has been excluded; any degree of PYP uptake can occur in AL. The practice points recommend serum free light chains and serum and urine immunofixation. This does not replace a clinical diagnostic pathway.

practiceQuestions.stem: An oncology PET/CT shows intense FDG uptake in a focal lesion. Which conclusion is most defensible from uptake alone?

options.text: The lesion is malignant because FDG uptake is tumor-specific.
The uptake identifies increased tracer accumulation but is not specific by itself; correlate with pattern, anatomy, history and other evidence.
The lesion is infection because tumors do not take up FDG.
The uptake proves a treatment response.

practiceQuestions.rationale: FDG uptake can occur in malignancy, inflammation and physiologic processes. Interpretation requires the tracer and clinical question, image quality, CT localization and comparison. The IAEA gallery explicitly includes non-malignant findings and alternative tracers.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes PSMA PET selection from a radioligand-therapy decision?

options.text: A positive PSMA PET automatically makes every patient eligible for 177Lu-PSMA therapy.
PSMA PET is an approved imaging basis for selecting patients under indication-specific FDA criteria, but treatment eligibility also depends on the applicable label and clinical assessment.
Post-therapy 177Lu imaging is interchangeable with baseline PSMA PET selection imaging.
PSMA PET can only be used for bone metastases.

practiceQuestions.rationale: FDA updates describe PSMA-positive populations and selection with Locametz or another approved PSMA PET product for specific Pluvicto indications. The scan is not a universal therapy authorization; current label, disease state, other criteria and clinical review apply. Diagnostic and post-treatment imaging have distinct purposes.

practiceQuestions.stem: A public imaging lecture provides a scanner quality-control tutorial. What does viewing it establish for an independent learner?

options.text: Competence to operate the camera independently.
Completion of NRC authorized-user hours and case experience.
Exposure to a teaching resource only; supervised practice, local qualification and required training remain separate.
Eligibility for ABNM certification.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A recording is an educational resource. ABNM and NRC-related training requirements include formal education and supervised experiential requirements; a public tutorial does not document those. The ABNM blueprint and exam are distinct from training eligibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: In the published ABNM certification exam blueprint, which major category has the largest listed share of questions?

options.text: Core
Cardiovascular
Oncology
Therapy

practiceQuestions.rationale: The current ABNM blueprint page lists oncology at 34% of certification exam questions, followed by cardiovascular at 16%; this is a blueprint distribution, not a prediction of individual readiness or a guarantee of exam format permanence.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has a new PSMA PET study and an earlier diagnostic CT. What is a defensible first step when uptake appears anatomically discordant?

options.text: Assume the tracer has failed and discard all images.
Review image quality, registration and attenuation-correction effects, tracer-specific biodistribution, and anatomic localization before assigning meaning.
Report metastasis based only on the maximum standardized uptake value.
Reconstruct the clinical images in a personal repository for later teaching.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Hybrid image artifacts and tracer-specific biodistribution should be assessed before interpretation. A single SUV is not a diagnosis; images are not to be copied or rehosted without rights. Public TCIA files are linked for lawful case study under their own access, license and citation rules.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about the Johns Hopkins offering in this packet is supported by current official programme pages?

options.text: The exact directory-labelled Molecular Imaging Residency page itself supplies a complete public curriculum and guaranteed dual-board eligibility.

The directory label describes combined radiology and nuclear medicine training; the current Nuclear Medicine Residency page separately states ACGME accreditation and ABNM exam qualification, while its PET/CT clinical fellowship is ACGME-equivalent and for physicians with a completed diagnostic radiology or nuclear medicine residency.
The PET/CT clinical fellowship is a standalone molecular imaging board certification.
The programme publicly lists exact video hours and patient case volumes.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The directory record and current departmental page have distinct naming and scope. Neither publicly supplies a complete official lecture ledger or guarantees certification; the current page states ACGME accreditation for NM residency, an ACGME-equivalent PET/CT clinical fellowship, and its prerequisites.

practiceQuestions.stem: A self-study learner completes this 36-hour video curriculum. What credential outcome follows?

options.text: The learner automatically becomes eligible for ABNM certification.
The learner receives an accredited residency-equivalent certificate.
No board eligibility, licensure, authorized-user status, supervised case volume or clinical competence follows; those depend on external requirements and training.
The learner can administer radiopharmaceutical therapy under this curriculum.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABNM eligibility depends on specific clinical preparation, ACGME-equivalent training and other criteria; authorized-user requirements add supervised hours/cases. A self-study curriculum cannot replace those, nor grant licensure or procedure authorization.

title: Molecular Imaging in Medicine Track
level: Combined clinical physician residency track (Emory MIM4/MIM5); independent self-study course-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Intended level: physicians, residents/fellows and advanced health-science learners; assumes prior anatomy, physiology, basic pathology, medical terminology and introductory radiation concepts. This is not a medical-school or residency curriculum substitute.
Learners should be able to distinguish diagnostic imaging from therapy, and image interpretation from radiopharmaceutical administration or radiation-safety work.

All patient-care decisions, image interpretations, tracer selection, therapy, dosage, protocoling, emergency escalation and equipment operation require licensed, supervised, credentialed personnel and local policy. No independent clinical use is authorized.
objectives: Explain the role and limitations of molecular imaging and pair a clinical question with a defensible modality/tracer choice at a conceptual level.

Integrate cardiovascular, endocrine, neurologic, oncologic, infection/inflammation, musculoskeletal, pulmonary, gastrointestinal and urinary nuclear-medicine domains with relevant anatomy and clinical context.
Distinguish diagnostic imaging from radionuclide therapy, recognize safety and patient-selection considerations, and check date-sensitive indications against current labels/guidelines.
Separate ABR and ABNM certification routes from ACGME training requirements and identify where case logs, supervised competence, licensure or NRC requirements cannot be learned through open videos.
Use authentic educational cases only through source links, honoring access/licensing terms and never copying patient records or unlicensed clinical images.

assessment.rubric: For each answer, award credit for accurate reasoning, appropriate uncertainty, correct source use and scope/safety awareness; do not award credit for an unsupported diagnosis or patient-management directive.

studyHours.plan: Suggested independent-study plan: 48–60 study hours total (36 hours target public lecture curriculum, plus 12–24 hours reading, retrieval practice and case reflection). This is a planning estimate, not measured instruction, clinical training, credit or accreditation.
studyHours.durationRule: Only unique publicly available recorded lectures with observed source-derived durations count. Planned original clips, unknown durations, repeated material, rotations and text readings do not count. The verified videos below are classified as shared technical foundation only; no specialty-clinical lecture hours are verified, so the track remains materially incomplete.

mapping.name: Molecular Imaging in Medicine (MIM) Track — four-year (MIM4) and five-year research-enhanced (MIM5) pathways within Diagnostic Radiology Residency
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: The current public page calls this a combined diagnostic radiology and nuclear medicine molecular imaging residency track. It describes at least 32 months of diagnostic radiology and 16 months of nuclear medicine; MIM5 adds dedicated research/flex time. Residents may apply during R1/R2; transfer residents may be considered. It lists a journal club, lecture series, weekly Research-in-Progress conferences and four one-week learning modules (radiochemistry/radiopharmacy mandatory, three selected). These public details do not disclose a complete lecture archive, rotation-by-rotation schedule, all cases, case volumes or exact didactic hours. The linked handbook is dated 2016 and is treated as historical, not a current controlling curriculum.

medical.boardStatus: Emory’s current public MIM page describes a combined diagnostic radiology and nuclear medicine residency track, with a stated goal of dual ABR/ABNM board eligibility/certification. The current ABNM rules allow an integrated diagnostic radiology route with 16 months (64 weeks) of nuclear medicine training during a four-year DR residency, subject to all requirements and board review. The ABR and ABNM are separate certifying boards and separate examinations/certifications. ABR exam format is in transition: the ABR page describes computer-based Certifying Exams in 2026–2027 and an oral exam after 2027. Individual eligibility is determined by the boards and accredited training, not by this course.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent self-study course confers no ABR/ABNM eligibility, ACGME training credit, medical licensure, board certification, supervised interpretation/procedure competence, clinical case logs, NRC authorized-user status, radiation-safety authorization or institutional credentialing. The ABNM/NRC pathway requires supervised hands-on work, specified experience and attestation; online learning cannot supply these. Confirm current eligibility and requirements directly with ABR, ABNM, ACGME, the programme and applicable regulators. No exam pass or readiness is promised.

officialProgrammes.name: Molecular Imaging in Medicine (MIM) Track — four-year (MIM4) and five-year research-enhanced (MIM5) pathways within Diagnostic Radiology Residency
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: The current public page calls this a combined diagnostic radiology and nuclear medicine molecular imaging residency track. It describes at least 32 months of diagnostic radiology and 16 months of nuclear medicine; MIM5 adds dedicated research/flex time. Residents may apply during R1/R2; transfer residents may be considered. It lists a journal club, lecture series, weekly Research-in-Progress conferences and four one-week learning modules (radiochemistry/radiopharmacy mandatory, three selected). These public details do not disclose a complete lecture archive, rotation-by-rotation schedule, all cases, case volumes or exact didactic hours. The linked handbook is dated 2016 and is treated as historical, not a current controlling curriculum.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Institutional public programme page supports Emory programme identity, named MIM4/MIM5 options and broad training structure, not full unpublished didactics or clinical volume. ACGME sources specify specialty programme requirements, not Emory’s actual delivery. ABR/ABNM pages specify their own certification pathways; neither turns this self-study course into training. IAEA videos and publications are public educational resources, not Emory/Harvard/JHU course materials. No Harvard or Johns Hopkins MIM-specific variant was identified in this packet; this MED-069 item is specifically the Emory MIM track.
sourceCaveats: The original packet’s inclusion note called this a supplementary non-physician track. That classification conflicts with the current official Emory MIM page, which explicitly calls it a combined diagnostic radiology and nuclear medicine molecular imaging residency track. This curriculum follows the official current Emory page and corrects the packet’s classification; the research-enhanced MIM5 component is not itself a separate physician specialty or board.

Emory’s page reports dual board eligibility/certification as a track goal. ABR and ABNM independently control eligibility and certification; no guarantee applies to a particular trainee. The examinations are separate.
