medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a conceptual PET/CT review, what is the most defensible first step before labeling an uptake focus abnormal?

options.text: Assume the hottest focus is malignant.
Confirm the clinical question and assess expected physiologic biodistribution and study quality.
Use SUV alone to assign histology.
Ignore the CT component.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Interpretation begins with indication and technical adequacy; expected distribution and anatomic correlation help prevent overcalling. Uptake intensity alone does not establish etiology.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which technical issue can undermine PET/CT interpretation even when the biological uptake pattern seems plausible?

options.text: Misregistration or attenuation-correction artifact.
Availability of prior imaging.
A clearly documented indication.
A normal physiologic pattern.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The IAEA physics seminar series covers PET/CT and SPECT/CT artifacts and reconstruction. A technical artifact can mimic or obscure uptake and must be considered.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional educational PET/CT vignette shows an FDG-avid focus without clinical context. What is the soundest conclusion?

options.text: FDG avidity proves cancer.
The finding needs anatomic, clinical and differential correlation; FDG uptake is not uniquely malignant.
No differential is needed if uptake is intense.
The scan determines treatment automatically.

practiceQuestions.rationale: FDG uptake can arise from malignancy, inflammation and physiologic or benign processes; correlation and uncertainty are essential.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately distinguishes open online education from NRC authorized-user qualification?

options.text: Any physician who watches a radiation-safety lecture becomes an authorized user.
The pathway includes specified training plus supervised work experience and required attestations; this course cannot confer it.
Only an exam is required.
A free video replaces all clinical experience.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABNM explains NRC training/experience requirements and supervision/attestation. Online study cannot replace hands-on supervised experience or the regulator’s requirements.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner sees a focus on a hybrid PET/CT. Which practice best incorporates the anatomic component?

options.text: Ignore CT because PET is molecular.
Correlate the metabolic focus with the anatomic CT finding, quality and clinical context, while retaining a differential.
Call it malignant if the CT component is abnormal.
Assume fused images have perfect registration.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME requires correlation with other imaging and clinical data; hybrid imaging still has quality, registration and specificity limitations.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about ABR and ABNM certification for the Emory MIM track is correct?

options.text: They are a single combined board exam.
ABR and ABNM are separate boards with distinct eligibility and certification requirements; the programme page describes a combined track goal.
Self-study automatically makes a graduate board eligible.
MIM5 research alone confers board eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Emory describes combined DR/NM training and dual board eligibility/certification goals, but ABR and ABNM control separate pathways and exam eligibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is the safest way to apply a date-sensitive radioligand therapy indication in education?

options.text: Assume any PSMA-avid tumor is eligible.
Use the current FDA prescribing information and applicable guidelines, recognizing that patient selection and safety criteria are specific.
Treat diagnostic PET as a therapy order.
Use an old indication summary without checking its date.

practiceQuestions.rationale: FDA indications are defined by disease state and treatment context and can change; diagnostic imaging alone does not establish treatment eligibility or replace label review.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which reasoning best distinguishes conceptual cardiac PET interpretation from patient-care activity?

options.text: A learner may supervise stress testing after watching an atlas.
A learner may compare perfusion and metabolic imaging concepts, but stress supervision and care require appropriate training, licensing and supervision.
A static image determines the complete clinical plan.
The atlas substitutes for case volumes.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Cardiac PET educational materials support self-study only; ACGME/board and licensure requirements are separate and include supervised clinical responsibilities.

practiceQuestions.stem: For a fictional endocrine nuclear imaging vignette, which response is most appropriate when scan findings are discordant with laboratory context?

options.text: Declare the scan definitive and ignore laboratory results.
Reconcile method, indication, image quality, clinical/laboratory data and alternative explanations; state uncertainty.
Use uptake intensity to establish etiology.
Recommend therapy based on the educational case alone.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME requires correlation with clinical and laboratory data. The scenario is fictional and cannot justify real treatment advice.

practiceQuestions.stem: A molecular-imaging signal in a fictional musculoskeletal case may reflect infection or sterile inflammation. Which approach is best?

options.text: Treat tracer uptake as uniquely infectious.
Build a differential and correlate with history, labs, anatomy and other imaging; recognize tracer nonspecificity.
Avoid reviewing clinical context.
Make an independent treatment decision.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Molecular imaging findings can overlap across etiologies. The educational goal is differential reasoning and correlation, not independent patient management.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the appropriate lesson from pediatric nuclear medicine image optimization resources?

options.text: A generic online course supplies patient-specific pediatric dose orders.
Pediatric acquisition and interpretation need age/context-aware optimization under current protocols and qualified supervision.
Adult and pediatric image interpretation are identical in every respect.
A learner may independently operate equipment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Pediatric imaging requires careful optimization and context; public educational material is not authority for individualized protocols or unsupervised practice.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes diagnostic PSMA PET from post-therapy Lu-177 imaging?

options.text: They are interchangeable examinations with the same tracer and purpose.
They serve different clinical contexts and use different radiopharmaceuticals; interpretation and indications must be kept distinct.
Any diagnostic scan authorizes therapy.
Post-therapy imaging is never needed.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Diagnostic target-expression imaging and post-therapy distribution/imaging are distinct modalities and clinical questions; treatment requires current label and clinical eligibility assessment.

objectives: Describe size, depth, compartment, margins, signal and enhancement pattern.
Recognize features that increase concern and prompt MRI/referral.
Avoid unplanned biopsy/excision and distinguish imaging impression from tissue diagnosis.
State limits of ultrasound and MRI where tissue remains necessary.
topics: Mass characterization by compartment, signal, enhancement and risk; image-guided workup principles.
units.casePractice: Draft an imaging-only fictional soft-tissue mass report plus a safety checklist for referral and biopsy planning.
units.assessment: Draft an imaging-only fictional soft-tissue mass report plus a safety checklist for referral and biopsy planning.

units.title: Bone, joint and soft-tissue infection
objectives: Identify marrow, cortical, joint and soft-tissue findings and important mimics.
Apply SSR-consensus terminology and graded likelihood language.
Recognize that MRI alone does not always establish microbiological diagnosis.
Communicate high-risk findings and limitations promptly to the clinical team.
topics: Osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, abscess, diabetic foot and infection terminology.
boardDomains: Infection 5–10%; bone, soft-tissue, joint and spinal infection
units.casePractice: Rewrite an intentionally overconfident fictional report using precise consensus terms and explicit differential/uncertainty.
units.assessment: Rewrite an intentionally overconfident fictional report using precise consensus terms and explicit differential/uncertainty.

units.title: Spine, marrow, osteonecrosis and systemic disease
objectives: Recognize common degenerative, traumatic, infectious and neoplastic spinal patterns.
Distinguish marrow replacement from reconversion and other common signal mimics.
Identify osteonecrosis features and stage cautiously.
Use clinical history and comparison imaging to reduce overcalling.
topics: MSK spine, marrow infiltration, osteonecrosis, hematologic/metabolic change and mimics.
boardDomains: Spine; marrow up to 5%; osteonecrosis; hematologic/endocrine/metabolic disease
units.casePractice: Write a differential table for a fictional marrow signal pattern and identify features that would change urgency.
units.assessment: Write a differential table for a fictional marrow signal pattern and identify features that would change urgency.

units.title: Pediatric MSK and developmental imaging
objectives: Differentiate expected age-related ossification from injury and disease.
Recognize common pediatric fracture patterns and growth plate involvement.
Describe developmental hip/foot and skeletal dysplasia concepts without unsupported diagnosis.
Use age-specific imaging and dose considerations.
topics: Normal growth and ossification, congenital variants, pediatric trauma and selected pediatric tumors/infection.
boardDomains: Adult and pediatric axial/appendicular scope; congenital up to 5%; pediatric trauma
units.casePractice: Interpret two openly linked teaching cases (one pediatric, one adult) and note developmental-stage caveats.
units.assessment: Interpret two openly linked teaching cases (one pediatric, one adult) and note developmental-stage caveats.

units.title: Postoperative imaging, hardware, prosthesis and bone density
objectives: Describe implant alignment, loosening, fracture, infection and soft-tissue complications.
Distinguish expected postoperative appearance from a potential complication.
Explain role/limitations of radiography, CT and MRI artifact reduction.
Recognize DEXA positioning, interpretation and common artifacts at a high level.
topics: Implants, expected postoperative appearances, complication patterns, arthrography and DEXA.
boardDomains: Postoperative up to 5%; implants/prosthesis; procedure safety; bone density
units.casePractice: Create a fictional post-arthroplasty structured report and peer-score it using the rubric below.
units.assessment: Create a fictional post-arthroplasty structured report and peer-score it using the rubric below.

units.title: Image-guided procedures, safety, quality and board synthesis
objectives: Identify indications, contraindications, consent, safety checks and complications conceptually.
Describe required supervision and limits of didactic-only procedural learning.
Integrate quality, communication, radiation safety and uncertainty into a case discussion.
Map acquired knowledge to ABR MSK blueprint while recognizing that this is not an exam predictor.
topics: Arthrography, aspiration/injection, biopsy principles, professionalism, safety and final board-style integration.
boardDomains: ACGME-supervised arthrogram/injection/biopsy; ABR procedures and safety; noninterpretive skills
units.casePractice: Deliver a 5-minute case conference using a fictional scenario; no procedural performance or unsupervised patient advice.
units.assessment: Deliver a 5-minute case conference using a fictional scenario; no procedural performance or unsupervised patient advice.

assignment.name: Integrated linked-case portfolio (self-study only)
deliverables: 12 short unit learning artifacts: structured report, differential/next step, or comparison matrix; no patient identifiers or copied images.
One final fictional case conference following the 5-minute template: question, salient findings, differential, recommendation/uncertainty, communication.
A self-reflection identifying two blueprint topic gaps and a source-based study plan.
assignment.casePolicy: Cases are links to repository-hosted authentic educational cases. Do not copy images or patient records. If access/permission unclear, choose text-only questions or another licensed source. No real-patient care decisions.

assessment.format: 10 original multiple-choice questions plus unit assignments; criterion-based learning checks only, no validated prediction of board passage.
assessment.suggestedThreshold: 80% for self-remediation only; not validated or credential-bearing. Repeat missed concepts with source reading.

rubric.proficient: Accurately states modality, site, morphology and salient positives/negatives.
Ranks plausible alternatives using distribution, age and context; avoids overcalling.
Chooses guideline-supported next step, identifies urgency and states limitations.
Cites authoritative source, uses respectful uncertainty, protects privacy and recognizes supervision limits.

studyHours.estimate: 120–160 hours of independent study over 12–16 weeks, excluding verified video runtime; a planning estimate, not a measured workload or clinical experience.
studyHours.schedule: One unit per week (reading, linked case practice and assessment); allocate additional time to weak blueprint areas.

unitMap.text: Approach, anatomy, modality choice and reporting
coveredTopics: Normal anatomy/variants, indications and limitations, structured search pattern, protocol and report communication.

unitMap.text: Trauma, fracture characterization and emergency imaging
coveredTopics: Acute and chronic trauma across adult/pediatric patients, occult injury, fracture healing and complication.

unitMap.text: Shoulder, elbow, wrist and hand
coveredTopics: Regional anatomy and common tendon, labral, ligament, instability and degenerative patterns.

unitMap.text: Hip, pelvis and lower-extremity joints
coveredTopics: Hip/pelvic alignment and adult/pediatric hip disease; knee, ankle and foot internal derangement.

unitMap.text: Arthropathies, inflammatory disease and metabolic bone
coveredTopics: Degenerative, inflammatory, crystal, neuropathic and systemic disease patterns.

unitMap.text: Bone tumors and tumor-like lesions
coveredTopics: Benign/aggressive lesion assessment, age/location/matrix, soft tissue extension, metastases and safe workup.

unitMap.text: Soft-tissue masses and tumors
coveredTopics: Mass characterization by compartment, signal, enhancement and risk; image-guided workup principles.

unitMap.text: Bone, joint and soft-tissue infection
coveredTopics: Osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, abscess, diabetic foot and infection terminology.

unitMap.text: Spine, marrow, osteonecrosis and systemic disease
coveredTopics: MSK spine, marrow infiltration, osteonecrosis, hematologic/metabolic change and mimics.

unitMap.text: Pediatric MSK and developmental imaging
coveredTopics: Normal growth and ossification, congenital variants, pediatric trauma and selected pediatric tumors/infection.

unitMap.text: Postoperative imaging, hardware, prosthesis and bone density
coveredTopics: Implants, expected postoperative appearances, complication patterns, arthrography and DEXA.

unitMap.text: Image-guided procedures, safety, quality and board synthesis
coveredTopics: Arthrography, aspiration/injection, biopsy principles, professionalism, safety and final board-style integration.

topicGaps: Emory channel inventory remains poorly mapped: the 26 speaker-only lecture titles have no defensible unit-specific mapping; those hours are included in the external runtime total, not assigned to topics.
The requested 36-hour observed-video floor is met by unique public recordings; hours above the floor are not evidence of complete topic coverage or competence.

No dedicated independently verified lecture block was mapped for MSK MRI infection nomenclature/diabetic-foot mimics; the full written SSR consensus and authored episode address concepts, but cases and clinical correlation remain necessary.

Arthropathies are only partly addressed by a case-focused hand recording; broad inflammatory, crystal, neuropathic and metabolic bone patterns and DEXA interpretation need additional source-backed teaching.
Spine trauma and procedural metastasis recordings do not constitute comprehensive diagnostic spine, marrow replacement/reconversion, osteonecrosis, or systemic marrow teaching.

Pediatric coverage from congenital dysplasia, osteoid-osteoma, and trauma recordings is incomplete for normal ossification, growth-plate injury, pediatric infection, tumors, and age-specific protocols.
The Soft Tissue-RADS webinar covers a standardized framework but does not replace full lesion-specific characterization, local referral protocols, histology, or specialist assessment.
Procedure recordings are conceptual educational material only; no supervised practice, credential, privilege, patient-specific recommendation, or procedural competence is offered.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

officialProgrammes.name: Musculoskeletal Imaging Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official Emory programme page says one-year fellowship in diagnostic and procedural orthopedic imaging; clinical service, teaching, scholarly activity, radiography/CT/MR/US, bone/joint/soft tissue/spine, image-guided procedures, weekly case conference and multidisciplinary conferences. Emory explicitly links the MSK video channel. The page does not publish a complete formal curriculum, all rotations, detailed topic schedule, individual case/volume metrics, or the ACGME accreditation status of this exact track. The fellowship index states Emory has both ACGME-accredited and non-accredited fellowships without identifying which applies here. Emory’s link to a channel does not make channel publisher official: channel describes itself as unofficial.

medical.programmeSourceScope: One distinct official physician clinical fellowship offering, Emory University School of Medicine; not a residency, combined program, generic directory category, or research-only postdoctoral supplement. Programme has diagnostic and procedural clinical activity, but page does not establish ACGME accreditation. Supplementary content is limited to self-study of noncredentialed theory; no separate physics/informatics track is being represented.
sourceCaveats: Emory identifies the programme as a one-year clinical/procedural fellowship. Accreditation status for this exact programme could not be verified from public Emory listing, so this record does not assert it is ACGME accredited.
Emory’s fellowship page links the channel, but the channel labels itself unofficial. Do not attribute its lectures as Emory-authored/endorsed without direct confirmation.

Saved channel metadata in the prior research archive lists 26 distinct unique IDs and durations; freshly fetched channel page shows the public channel and 26 videos and directly exposes runtimes for its first six entries. YouTube bot/PO-token checks blocked later direct watch-page probes, so current individual playback/free stream availability was not reconfirmed. The count is published transparently with that caveat and should be rechecked before launch.
Video titles expose speaker names but not topics; topic-level mappings are unknown. Do not count one talk under multiple specific topics or reuse a video ID.
The 2019 ACR acute knee trauma narrative is openly linked but may be superseded; check ACR for updates before clinical application.
The current ABR MSK blueprint is an exam-content map, not the ACGME fellowship curriculum. ACGME standards describe accredited supervised GME, not this independent course.
MedPix landing page displays a federal funding lapse/service currency notice as observed on the checked date.
Clinical content and questions have not been reviewed by a human clinician. No diagnosis, patient care, or procedure advice is supplied.

topicGaps: Emory channel inventory remains poorly mapped: the 26 speaker-only lecture titles have no defensible unit-specific mapping; those hours are included in the external runtime total, not assigned to topics.
The requested 36-hour observed-video floor is met by unique public recordings; hours above the floor are not evidence of complete topic coverage or competence.

No dedicated independently verified lecture block was mapped for MSK MRI infection nomenclature/diabetic-foot mimics; the full written SSR consensus and authored episode address concepts, but cases and clinical correlation remain necessary.

Arthropathies are only partly addressed by a case-focused hand recording; broad inflammatory, crystal, neuropathic and metabolic bone patterns and DEXA interpretation need additional source-backed teaching.
Spine trauma and procedural metastasis recordings do not constitute comprehensive diagnostic spine, marrow replacement/reconversion, osteonecrosis, or systemic marrow teaching.

Pediatric coverage from congenital dysplasia, osteoid-osteoma, and trauma recordings is incomplete for normal ossification, growth-plate injury, pediatric infection, tumors, and age-specific protocols.
The Soft Tissue-RADS webinar covers a standardized framework but does not replace full lesion-specific characterization, local referral protocols, histology, or specialist assessment.
Procedure recordings are conceptual educational material only; no supervised practice, credential, privilege, patient-specific recommendation, or procedural competence is offered.

practiceQuestions.stem: A skeletally mature adult has focal knee tenderness and an effusion after an acute twisting injury. What is the usual initial imaging modality?

options.text: MRI without contrast
Radiography
CT with IV contrast
Bone scan

practiceQuestions.rationale: Radiography is generally the initial imaging test after clinical assessment for acute knee trauma when imaging is indicated. MRI or CT is selected for a subsequent, defined unresolved question.

practiceQuestions.stem: Knee radiographs show no fracture, but occult fracture or internal derangement remains suspected in a skeletally mature patient. Which next examination is rated usually appropriate by the linked ACR variant?

options.text: MRI knee without IV contrast
MRI knee with and without contrast
Bone scan with SPECT/CT
Ultrasound knee

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ACR acute-trauma variant supports MRI without contrast as usually appropriate after negative radiographs when occult fracture/internal derangement is suspected. CT without contrast may be appropriate for selected bony questions.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best reflects the ACR pathway for acute knee trauma?

options.text: MRI is first-line for every acute twist
CT with IV contrast is mandatory after normal films
Radiographs are usually initial; subsequent imaging depends on the remaining question
Ultrasound excludes occult fracture

practiceQuestions.rationale: Radiographs are usually the initial examination when indicated; MRI/CT selection depends on whether occult marrow/soft-tissue injury or fracture characterization is the issue.

practiceQuestions.stem: A diabetic-foot MRI shows fluid-sensitive marrow hyperintensity adjacent to an ulcer, but T1 marrow signal is not clearly replaced. What is a cautious SSR-consistent report approach?

options.text: Call osteomyelitis definitively in every case
Use high-likelihood language with clinical correlation rather than claiming proof
Call this osteitis, which the consensus prefers
Exclude infection because T1 is preserved

practiceQuestions.rationale: SSR consensus recommends “high likelihood of osteomyelitis” for fluid-sensitive marrow signal adjacent to an ulcer/abscess/sinus tract even if T1 signal criteria are incomplete; imaging is not microbiologic proof.

practiceQuestions.stem: What wording does the SSR consensus discourage as nonspecific when describing a suspected soft-tissue infection on MRI?

options.text: Cellulitis
Soft tissue abscess
Phlegmon
Intramuscular abscess

practiceQuestions.rationale: The consensus discourages “phlegmon” and recommends specific terms such as cellulitis, myositis, or fasciitis without abscess when applicable.

practiceQuestions.stem: An incidentally found solitary adult bone lesion is discovered on CT/MRI. Which framework is specifically designed to standardize risk assessment/management of that scenario?

options.text: PI-RADS
Bone-RADS
LI-RADS
Lung-RADS

practiceQuestions.rationale: The SSR Bone Reporting and Data System (Bone-RADS) white paper addresses incidental solitary bone lesions in adults on CT/MRI. It does not replace clinical assessment or histology.

practiceQuestions.stem: A bone lesion has aggressive imaging features and needs biopsy. Which principle is safest?

options.text: Perform an unplanned biopsy immediately
Coordinate the biopsy route with the definitive treating tumor service
Biopsy only after radiotherapy
Use imaging appearance as definitive histology

practiceQuestions.rationale: Biopsy planning should be coordinated with the team that will manage a suspected bone/soft-tissue tumor; avoid an unplanned tract or excision that can compromise definitive care. This is a safety principle, not a diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: An MRI shows diffuse marrow edema-like signal around a joint. What is the strongest general reasoning approach?

options.text: Treat edema as specific for one diagnosis
Integrate distribution, T1 signal, cortical/soft-tissue findings, clinical context and alternatives
Report osteomyelitis without context
Ignore normal radiographs

practiceQuestions.rationale: Marrow edema is a pattern rather than a diagnosis; integrate morphology, other sequences/findings and clinical information. The SSR infection consensus explicitly addresses mimics and graded likelihood.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which content statement accurately reflects the ABR DR MSK exam blueprint?

options.text: It contains only MRI and no radiographs
Trauma is a weighted content area; the MSK domain spans radiography, fluoroscopy, US, CT and MRI
It is a separate MSK subspecialty certificate exam
It excludes pediatric imaging

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABR core blueprint defines MSK imaging across radiographic, fluoroscopic, ultrasound, CT and MRI modalities, and publishes trauma as 20–25% of the MSK domain.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is a valid claim about completing this independent course?

options.text: It establishes ABR board eligibility
It confers supervised procedure competence
It replaces an accredited fellowship
It provides self-study only and grants none of these credentials or privileges

practiceQuestions.rationale: An independent online curriculum cannot replace medical education, accredited supervised clinical training, licensure, board eligibility or procedural competence.

title: Neuroradiology Fellowship
prerequisites: Intended for physicians who have completed diagnostic radiology residency or equivalent foundational physician radiology training; the course is not residency substitute.
Working knowledge of neuroanatomy, CT/MR physics, contrast/safety principles, cross-sectional interpretation and general radiology reporting.
Recommended: prior diagnostic radiology residency; non-physician learners may use conceptual modules but must not interpret clinical studies or act clinically.
objectives: Use a reproducible approach to brain, spine and head-and-neck CT/MR interpretation.

Demonstrate advanced modality/sequence and artifact reasoning, including vascular and diffusion imaging.

Construct concise, uncertainty-calibrated educational impressions and discuss cases responsibly.

topicGaps: Verified free long-form lecture hours remain 0 of the 36-hour target: all ten inherited video records lack observed runtime and independently verified free playback. No new candidate met both inclusion criteria.

AAR and ASNR catalogues list relevant brain, spine, pediatric and head-and-neck topics, but item-level playback/runtime evidence was not available from the accessible public pages; these remain uncounted research leads.

Topic-specific instruction remains insufficient for spine trauma/fracture classifications, degenerative nomenclature and hardware failure; spinal infection/inflammatory arthropathy, spinal neoplasm and vascular disease; detailed head-and-neck regional pathology, nodal/staging systems, treatment effects and temporal bone; pediatric protocols and age-specific disorders; and detailed brain infection, congenital/perinatal, epilepsy, trauma, advanced imaging and disease-specific response criteria.

Five complete source-grounded original teaching scripts address introductory interpretive method and selected vascular brain, brain tumor, spinal cord and head-and-neck reasoning gaps. They are scripted only, not rendered or counted; they do not close the remaining topic or hour gaps.

The 36-hour target remains infeasible as verified public video in this research pass. The existing module-minute plans are unproduced placeholders; additional academically reviewed production and runtime/access checks are required before any hour can be credited.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardNames: American Board of Radiology (ABR) Neuroradiology Subspecialty Certification / Neuroradiology Subspecialty Exam
medical.boardStatus: A distinct ABR neuroradiology subspecialty examination and continuous subspecialty certificate exist for eligible diplomates; it is not a primary specialty board.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: ABR eligibility is governed by current ABR rules, including prerequisite diagnostic/general/IR-DR certification, an eligible ACGME/RCPSC neuroradiology fellowship (or alternate pathway), a valid license and additional practice/training criteria. This independent course confers none of these. Reconfirm current ABR policies and dates.

officialProgrammes.name: Neuroradiology Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page calls the diagnostic programme ACGME-accredited; public rotations cover complex inpatient/outpatient brain, spine, head/neck, pediatric, trauma, vascular/interventional exposure, evening/weekend work, conferences, journal club and research. Emory states 2026 expansion to 10 ACGME diagnostic fellows/year and optional second subspecialized year. Exact didactic/rotation hours are not publicly specified on pages reviewed. This is one physician fellowship—not residency, not a generic directory label, and not a combined programme. The optional year is a further institutional subspecialty year; exact focus/eligibility must be verified with Emory.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Packet assigned one Emory physician neuroradiology fellowship. Research verified Emory and ABR/ACGME; no separate Harvard/JHU offering was assigned or asserted. Exact Emory offering retained; 2026 optional second year described only as an Emory option, not a distinct physician specialty. Imaging informatics, imaging AI, physics and neurointerventional procedures are complementary content here, not substitutions for this fellowship or separate physician boards. No research-only or non-physician role is conflated.
sourceCaveats: Emory public source confirms a named ACGME-accredited diagnostic neuroradiology fellowship. It does not publish total educational or rotation hours; 2026 expansion/optional second year are time-sensitive and should be rechecked.

ABR names a separate neuroradiology subspecialty exam/certificate; this is not an independent primary specialty board or course credential. Eligibility requires separate prerequisites and license/practice conditions; verify current ABR policy.
ACGME programme requirements are accreditation standards, not ABR exam blueprint nor a transcript of Emory lectures.
Video runtime metadata extraction was blocked by the public platform anti-bot sign-in challenge; no browser/login workaround was attempted. Candidate links are not included in verified hours.
ASNR catalogue is dynamically rendered; page text verified but individual hosted playback/runtime could not be read.
Radiopaedia is free to view but rights do not equal permission to rehost. Verify individual case licensing and noncommercial status; use links only, no images/patient records copied.
No human clinical review performed; no guarantee of exam outcome, clinical competence or board eligibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 67-year-old with sudden aphasia has no hemorrhage on NCCT and subtle loss of insular gray-white differentiation. Best description?

options.text: Early ischemic change is possible; a negative hemorrhage screen does not exclude infarction.
Acute ischemia is excluded because no large hypodensity is seen.
The finding proves an embolic occlusion.
The scan alone establishes treatment eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Subtle early parenchymal changes may be present; NCCT does not exclude early ischemia or prove mechanism/eligibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which approach best evaluates possible true restricted diffusion?

options.text: DWI signal alone
DWI with ADC correlation
T1 post-contrast only
SWI alone

practiceQuestions.rationale: DWI hyperintensity should be correlated with ADC and technical/contextual information.

practiceQuestions.stem: CTA interpretation is degraded by poor arterial bolus timing. What is the best report practice?

options.text: Declare all vessels patent
Mention the limitation and qualify assessment of vessel opacification
Infer distal occlusion from clinical symptoms
Ignore technical quality

practiceQuestions.rationale: A technical limitation must be communicated; it constrains certainty.

practiceQuestions.stem: A diffusion abnormality crosses arterial territories in a patient with recent seizure. Which is most appropriate?

options.text: Label infarct as certain
Consider nonvascular mimics, including peri-ictal change, and integrate context
Exclude pathology
Diagnose tumor

practiceQuestions.rationale: Distribution and context should prompt a differential; diffusion restriction is not uniquely arterial ischemia.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which ABR study-guide section includes pediatric cases?

options.text: Only a separate pediatric exam
Pediatric cases are included in each of the three sections
Only brain

title: Neuroradiology Fellowship Program
level: Clinical physician fellowship (institutional analogue; independent self-study, not a clinical programme)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Diagnostic radiology foundations: cross-sectional anatomy, CT/MR acquisition, contrast, vascular imaging, radiation/MR safety, and structured reporting.
Physician-level background is assumed for interpretation, but the course is also an educational reference for radiology trainees under supervision; it is not an admission or credential pathway.
Prior supervised experience with clinical imaging workflow is helpful; not required for access to this independent content.
Do not use online material to diagnose oneself, treat a patient, perform a procedure, or substitute for supervision.
objectives: Select and critique neuroimaging protocols and describe major technical limitations.
Interpret and communicate educational cases across ABR brain, spine, and head-and-neck domains.
Construct prioritized differentials that integrate anatomy, modalities, age, clinical context and uncertainty.
Explain vascular, perfusion, diffusion, advanced MR, pediatric and post-treatment imaging caveats.
Appraise publicly accessible cases and scholarship lawfully without copying patient images or records.
Recognize that board certification, supervised clinical competence and actual ACGME fellowship are outside the scope of this course.

units.title: Neuroanatomy, protocols, physics, artifacts and reporting
units.level: Advanced radiology self-study; intended after diagnostic radiology foundations; not a substitute for supervised fellowship.
objectives: Describe key anatomic compartments and review planes
match CT/MR sequences and vascular protocols to a clinical question
identify common artifacts, technical limitations and urgent findings
structure an actionable, qualified report.
topics: Brain/spine/head-neck cross-sectional anatomy; CT/MR contrast; DWI/ADC, FLAIR, susceptibility, postcontrast, CTA/MRA/MRV; safety, artifacts, protocol selection; structured reporting and communication.
units.casePractice: Sequence-selection worksheet using fictional indications; identify artifact versus lesion on openly licensed teaching materials.
units.assessment: Protocol rationale 30%; anatomy and sequence labels 30%; artifacts/limitations 20%; report and escalation language 20%.

units.title: Neurovascular anatomy and imaging approach
units.level: Advanced radiology self-study; intended after diagnostic radiology foundations; not a substitute for supervised fellowship.
objectives: Trace arterial and venous anatomy
select CTA/CTV/MRA/MRV or catheter angiography in context
distinguish common variants from pathology
describe limitations without overcalling.
topics: Arterial territories; circle of Willis; venous sinuses; aneurysm, AVM, cavernous malformation, dissection, stenosis; image quality and incidental variants.
units.casePractice: Build a territory-to-modality comparison using linked teaching cases, without downloading images.
units.assessment: Anatomy mapping 35%; modality tradeoffs 25%; differential 25%; communication 15%.

units.title: Acute/subacute ischemia, hemorrhage and stroke imaging
units.level: Advanced radiology self-study; intended after diagnostic radiology foundations; not a substitute for supervised fellowship.
objectives: Systematically review noncontrast CT and multimodal CT/MRI in acute stroke
explain time-dependent appearances and perfusion maps
distinguish mimics and report uncertainty
separate imaging interpretation from treatment decisions.
topics: Early ischemic signs; hemorrhage; ASPECTS as a structured tool; CTA occlusion; perfusion core/penumbra concepts and artifacts; venous thrombosis; infarct evolution; mimics.
units.casePractice: Timed report on a public de-identified teaching case; map findings to presentation and state key limitations.
units.assessment: Systematic review 30%; lesion localization 25%; technique limitations 25%; safe concise communication 20%.

units.title: Brain neoplasms, mimics, treatment effects and advanced techniques
units.level: Advanced radiology self-study; intended after diagnostic radiology foundations; not a substitute for supervised fellowship.
objectives: Use age, compartment, signal, enhancement and diffusion to prioritize a differential
describe tumor extent and relevant anatomy
distinguish likely treatment effect from possible progression without unsupported certainty
explain limits of perfusion, spectroscopy, DTI, fMRI and PET.
topics: Primary and metastatic tumors; intra-axial/extra-axial; CNS lymphoma and mimics; current integrated WHO CNS taxonomy; edema, hemorrhage, treatment effects; perfusion, spectroscopy, functional and diffusion methods.
units.casePractice: Create a differential matrix with decisive/overlapping features from openly linked cases; cite current classification source.
units.assessment: Localization 20%; prioritized differential 30%; advanced-imaging caveats 25%; classification/communication 25%.

units.title: Infection, inflammation, demyelination and white-matter disease
units.level: Advanced radiology self-study; intended after diagnostic radiology foundations; not a substitute for supervised fellowship.
objectives: Integrate host context, distribution, enhancement and diffusion
construct a bounded differential for focal and diffuse disease
recognize urgent complications and state evidence gaps.
topics: Pyogenic and opportunistic infection; abscess; inflammatory and autoimmune disease; demyelination; MS-pattern criteria as an imaging support rather than standalone diagnosis; metabolic/genetic patterns.
units.casePractice: Compare 3 linked educational cases; explain the discriminating imaging pattern and at least two alternatives.
units.assessment: Pattern recognition 30%; differential 30%; sequence correlation 20%; uncertainty/safety 20%.

units.title: Trauma, emergency findings, hydrocephalus and intracranial pressure
units.level: Advanced radiology self-study; intended after diagnostic radiology foundations; not a substitute for supervised fellowship.
objectives: Apply a reproducible CT/MR review to acute trauma and raised-pressure presentations
recognize hemorrhage, mass effect, herniation, hydrocephalus and traumatic vascular injury
communicate time-critical findings.
topics: Extra-axial and intraparenchymal hemorrhage; skull base injury; diffuse axonal injury; edema/herniation; hydrocephalus; CSF pressure disorders; post-traumatic sequelae.
units.casePractice: Write a concise critical-result report from an open teaching case and formulate a differential, not a treatment order.
units.assessment: Search pattern 25%; critical finding 35%; differential 20%; communication 20%.

units.title: Pediatric, fetal, neonatal and developmental neuroradiology
units.level: Advanced radiology self-study; intended after diagnostic radiology foundations; not a substitute for supervised fellowship.
objectives: Describe age-dependent anatomy and modality selection
recognize developmental, congenital and perinatal patterns
avoid adult-only assumptions
identify limitations and escalation needs.
topics: Fetal MRI; neonatal cranial ultrasound; pediatric brain and spine tumors; malformations; neurocutaneous disease; pediatric stroke, infection and trauma.
units.casePractice: Age-specific case comparison through a public case library; no individual treatment advice.
units.assessment: Age-appropriate anatomy 25%; pattern 30%; modality 20%; differential and limits 25%.

units.title: Spine anatomy, degeneration, trauma and postoperative assessment
units.level: Advanced radiology self-study; intended after diagnostic radiology foundations; not a substitute for supervised fellowship.
objectives: Localize abnormalities to compartment and level
use consistent degenerative terminology
assess fracture pattern, stability indicators and hardware/postoperative appearance
report urgent neural compromise.
topics: Spinal cord, canal and foramina; disc disease; marrow; trauma classifications used by referring teams; infection; postsurgical changes; hardware and complications.
units.casePractice: Structured whole-spine reading exercise using public teaching cases and a non-diagnostic learner report.
units.assessment: Localization/level 30%; nomenclature 25%; differential 20%; red flags and report 25%.

units.title: Spinal neoplasms, infection, inflammatory and vascular disease
units.level: Advanced radiology self-study; intended after diagnostic radiology foundations; not a substitute for supervised fellowship.
objectives: Classify lesions as extradural, intradural-extramedullary or intramedullary
assess aggression and marrow/soft-tissue involvement
create a differential with relevant context
identify cord emergencies.
topics: Osseous and epidural neoplasm; intradural and intramedullary lesions; infection; inflammatory/demyelinating disease; ischemia, hemorrhage and malformations; lesion behavior and follow-up limits.
units.casePractice: Use a public linked case to map lesion compartment, signal and aggressive features; no image reuse.
units.assessment: Compartment 30%; differential 30%; red flags 20%; limitations 20%.

units.title: Spine image-guided procedures: interpretation, safety and governance
units.level: Advanced radiology self-study; intended after diagnostic radiology foundations; not a substitute for supervised fellowship.
objectives: Explain indications, image guidance, essential anatomy and risk language for common spinal procedures
recognize that text/video learning does not confer procedural competence
discuss consent, supervision and complication recognition.
topics: Lumbar puncture, myelography, biopsy, vertebral augmentation and other program-described procedures; fluoroscopic/CT guidance; contraindication screening, complications, quality and supervision.
units.casePractice: Write a procedure risk/benefit and image-guidance planning checklist for faculty review; never attempt unsupervised procedures.
units.assessment: Anatomy 25%; indication/contraindication reasoning 25%; safety 30%; professional scope boundary 20%.

units.title: Head and neck, skull base, orbit, sinonasal, temporal bone and special senses
units.level: Advanced radiology self-study; intended after diagnostic radiology foundations; not a substitute for supervised fellowship.
objectives: Choose modality and protocol by region/question
localize lesions to spaces and skull-base pathways
describe perineural spread, extent and treatment change
use differential rather than single-feature certainty.
topics: Orbits; sinonasal cavity; face; skull base/sella; CPA/IAC; temporal bone; suprahyoid/infrahyoid neck; nodes, infection, trauma, tumor, treatment change and reconstruction.
units.casePractice: Produce a compartment-based report on public case examples and compare pre/post-treatment imaging when available.
units.assessment: Regional anatomy 30%; modality choice 20%; extent/differential 30%; treatment change and limits 20%.

units.title: Vascular consultation, catheter angiography, quality, communication and scholarship
units.level: Advanced radiology self-study; intended after diagnostic radiology foundations; not a substitute for supervised fellowship.
objectives: Interpret and describe noninvasive and catheter-based cervicocerebral angiography at an educational level
conduct a case-based consultation
synthesize a journal article and communicate uncertainty
distinguish curriculum from actual supervised clinical requirements.
topics: Vascular neuroradiology; angiographic evaluation; M&M, journal club and interdisciplinary conference; quality/safety; critical appraisal, scholarly project and professional communication.
units.casePractice: Prepare a one-page journal club appraisal and an image-free interdisciplinary case presentation.
units.assessment: Evidence appraisal 25%; vascular reasoning 30%; consultation/report 25%; ethics/scope/safety 20%.

assignment.title: Image-free cross-domain case conference portfolio
assignment.instructions: Using a case that is explicitly free to view, document its canonical URL, access date, licence and access conditions. Do not download/re-host patient images. Submit an image-free structured report, a prioritized differential, modality-quality critique, one-page evidence appraisal, and a 5-minute verbal case conference using no protected images. Use fictional scenarios for original questions.

assessment.format: 12 unit formative checks, weekly image-free case write-ups, the assignment portfolio, and the 10 original practice items below.
assessment.passCriterion: For this independent course only, learner may set a formative target such as 80% on original items followed by remediation; this is not a board standard or pass prediction.
assessment.limitations: No psychometric validation, observed image interpretation, patient care evaluation, procedural assessment, faculty supervision, or human clinical review. Do not claim readiness or passing probability.

unitMap.text: Neuroanatomy, protocols, physics, artifacts and reporting
coveredTopics: Brain/spine/head-neck cross-sectional anatomy; CT/MR contrast; DWI/ADC, FLAIR, susceptibility, postcontrast, CTA/MRA/MRV; safety, artifacts, protocol selection; structured reporting and communication.

unitMap.text: Neurovascular anatomy and imaging approach
coveredTopics: Arterial territories; circle of Willis; venous sinuses; aneurysm, AVM, cavernous malformation, dissection, stenosis; image quality and incidental variants.

unitMap.text: Acute/subacute ischemia, hemorrhage and stroke imaging
coveredTopics: Early ischemic signs; hemorrhage; ASPECTS as a structured tool; CTA occlusion; perfusion core/penumbra concepts and artifacts; venous thrombosis; infarct evolution; mimics.

unitMap.text: Brain neoplasms, mimics, treatment effects and advanced techniques
coveredTopics: Primary and metastatic tumors; intra-axial/extra-axial; CNS lymphoma and mimics; current integrated WHO CNS taxonomy; edema, hemorrhage, treatment effects; perfusion, spectroscopy, functional and diffusion methods.

unitMap.text: Infection, inflammation, demyelination and white-matter disease
coveredTopics: Pyogenic and opportunistic infection; abscess; inflammatory and autoimmune disease; demyelination; MS-pattern criteria as an imaging support rather than standalone diagnosis; metabolic/genetic patterns.

unitMap.text: Trauma, emergency findings, hydrocephalus and intracranial pressure
coveredTopics: Extra-axial and intraparenchymal hemorrhage; skull base injury; diffuse axonal injury; edema/herniation; hydrocephalus; CSF pressure disorders; post-traumatic sequelae.

unitMap.text: Pediatric, fetal, neonatal and developmental neuroradiology
coveredTopics: Fetal MRI; neonatal cranial ultrasound; pediatric brain and spine tumors; malformations; neurocutaneous disease; pediatric stroke, infection and trauma.

unitMap.text: Spine anatomy, degeneration, trauma and postoperative assessment
coveredTopics: Spinal cord, canal and foramina; disc disease; marrow; trauma classifications used by referring teams; infection; postsurgical changes; hardware and complications.

unitMap.text: Spinal neoplasms, infection, inflammatory and vascular disease
coveredTopics: Osseous and epidural neoplasm; intradural and intramedullary lesions; infection; inflammatory/demyelinating disease; ischemia, hemorrhage and malformations; lesion behavior and follow-up limits.

unitMap.text: Spine image-guided procedures: interpretation, safety and governance
coveredTopics: Lumbar puncture, myelography, biopsy, vertebral augmentation and other program-described procedures; fluoroscopic/CT guidance; contraindication screening, complications, quality and supervision.

unitMap.text: Head and neck, skull base, orbit, sinonasal, temporal bone and special senses
coveredTopics: Orbits; sinonasal cavity; face; skull base/sella; CPA/IAC; temporal bone; suprahyoid/infrahyoid neck; nodes, infection, trauma, tumor, treatment change and reconstruction.

unitMap.text: Vascular consultation, catheter angiography, quality, communication and scholarship
coveredTopics: Vascular neuroradiology; angiographic evaluation; M&M, journal club and interdisciplinary conference; quality/safety; critical appraisal, scholarly project and professional communication.

topicGaps: The unique public duration-observed ledger totals 36.57361111 hours and clears the 36-hour media floor. This number represents linked existing public recordings only; episode scripts and future production plans do not count.

The expanded sources cover core modality/anatomy/pathology introductions, a large pediatric/developmental set, and selected adult head-and-neck topics. They are not a systematic current fellowship didactic series and differ in level, scope, quality and date.

Material topic gaps remain in systematic adult CT/MR protocol physics and artifacts; detailed vascular variants, CTA/CTV/MRA/MRV and catheter angiography; adult acute stroke/perfusion/hemorrhage; adult spine degeneration, trauma, neoplasm, infection and vascular disease; adult skull base/sinonasal/temporal bone/neck anatomy; advanced MR caveats; procedural risk/patient evaluation; contrast and sedation safety; structured reporting/consultation; quality, scholarship and observed clinical interpretation.

ACGME-required clinical experiences, case and procedure volumes, patient evaluation, supervision, feedback and professional practice cannot be acquired through recorded media. The ABR study guide is a general non-exhaustive topic outline. Hours are not evidence of competency, eligibility or board readiness.
ASNR Core Education offers a broad topic catalogue, but access terms and a complete free duration ledger were not established in this review; its unverified items remain uncounted.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician fellowship (institutional analogue; independent self-study, not a clinical programme)
boardNames: American Board of Radiology (ABR) — Neuroradiology Subspecialty Exam
medical.boardStatus: ABR offers a distinct neuroradiology subspecialty certification examination for eligible diplomates; not a separate initial physician specialty board. The ABR describes an image-rich, one-day computer-based examination of approximately 180 questions and approximately four hours. Exam guide divides content equally into brain, spine, and head & neck; pediatric cases appear throughout. Current exam format, timing, scoring and requirements can change.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: ABR information reviewed 2026-10-07 states that applicants need an ABR primary certificate in general radiology/diagnostic radiology or IR/DR; an ACGME- or RCPSC-accredited one-year neuroradiology fellowship; valid medical license; and one year of practice or additional approved training with at least one-third in neuroradiology (or qualifying alternate pathway). Verify directly with ABR. This independent course confers no board eligibility.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / Johns Hopkins Hospital
officialProgrammes.name: Neuroradiology Fellowship Program
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official directory calls it a one-year ACGME-accredited clinical fellowship. Current Department of Radiology page gives an 11-position one-year ACGME-accredited fellowship and describes an optional second-year advanced specialty/instructor route available to two fellows. The program identity and second-year route are the same offering, not separately deduplicated programs. The directory says unrestricted Maryland medical-license eligibility is needed for its second-year instructor program. No official independent Harvard variant is evidenced in this MED-072 packet.

medical.programmeSourceScope: One physician specialty fellowship, in the exact Johns Hopkins institutional variant supplied in the item packet. Official department page and general Johns Hopkins fellowship directory agree on one-year ACGME clinical status; the optional second instructor year is a distinct institutional advanced track, not a combined specialty or another board. Not a research-only fellowship, non-physician technologist programme, or generic directory category. This is a curriculum analogue, not the institution's curriculum and not a representation that learners can train there.
sourceCaveats: The current Hopkins page is the institutional source; positions, didactics, service volumes and technical offerings are institution-specific and can change. Public programme statements do not establish that this independent course duplicates their curriculum.

Hopkins reports average >5 scheduled didactic hours per week and historically most fellows read 5,000–6,000 studies; these are programme-reported figures and are not requirements, guarantees or course outcomes. ACGME requirements are separate standards.
ABR eligibility details and exam format are date-checked as of 2026-10-07 and may change; follow ABR's live page.

ASNR describes member resources and complimentary in-training membership for certain learner statuses. Do not imply that the fellowship curriculum is open without membership or count it as public hours.
YouTube is third-party hosting; public watch page without sign-in at review is not a promise of continued availability or license to republish.
No patient cases or diagnostic images have been copied into this deliverable; linked case image provenance and per-case rights remain source-side.
No human clinical review has been performed.

No Harvard clinical programme variant was supplied or verified for this specific specialty packet. Johns Hopkins variants are exact institutional representations of one clinical fellowship; optional instructor/advanced year is not a separate board or combined specialty.

topicGaps: The unique public duration-observed ledger totals 36.57361111 hours and clears the 36-hour media floor. This number represents linked existing public recordings only; episode scripts and future production plans do not count.

The expanded sources cover core modality/anatomy/pathology introductions, a large pediatric/developmental set, and selected adult head-and-neck topics. They are not a systematic current fellowship didactic series and differ in level, scope, quality and date.

Material topic gaps remain in systematic adult CT/MR protocol physics and artifacts; detailed vascular variants, CTA/CTV/MRA/MRV and catheter angiography; adult acute stroke/perfusion/hemorrhage; adult spine degeneration, trauma, neoplasm, infection and vascular disease; adult skull base/sinonasal/temporal bone/neck anatomy; advanced MR caveats; procedural risk/patient evaluation; contrast and sedation safety; structured reporting/consultation; quality, scholarship and observed clinical interpretation.

ACGME-required clinical experiences, case and procedure volumes, patient evaluation, supervision, feedback and professional practice cannot be acquired through recorded media. The ABR study guide is a general non-exhaustive topic outline. Hours are not evidence of competency, eligibility or board readiness.
ASNR Core Education offers a broad topic catalogue, but access terms and a complete free duration ledger were not established in this review; its unverified items remain uncounted.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult with abrupt focal neurologic deficit has a noncontrast CT without hemorrhage; a small region of insular gray-white blurring is suspected. What is the most defensible next interpretive step?

options.text: Call a definite large completed infarct from one subtle sign
Review systematically for early ischemic signs and correlate with CTA/MRI as clinically indicated
Exclude ischemia because there is no established hypodensity
Use a normal-appearing CT to exclude stroke

practiceQuestions.rationale: Early CT ischemic signs may be subtle; a negative or equivocal noncontrast CT does not by itself exclude ischemia. Additional imaging is determined by clinical pathway and local protocols; this educational question does not direct patient care.
practiceQuestions.status: Original educational item; not ABR content and not a validated predictor of performance.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional acute stroke case, CTP shows delayed Tmax in a region but technically poor arterial input and motion. What should a neuroradiology learner foreground?
